items.body: Photos by Lucie Schulze By Matty Bannond As sunlight weakened on the first day of autumn, visitors to this carefully curated event slipped their hands into a red-tartan sack full of plastic rings and dipped wooden wands into a pot of locally sourced honey. Symbolic gifts and gestures were the central focus of the evening. Each ceremonial act invited deeper contemplation of how shared experiences bind societies together. That reflective impulse was stirred by collective experiences and multi-layered stimuli. Many of those factors are fixed for each episode of the interdisciplinary Ritual series in north-west Germany, but each event culminates in a one-off concert. On September 1, saxophonist Hayden Chisholm and sound designer Robert Nacken transformed the interior of the Neu St. Alban church into an imagined beehive. Visual artist Natalia Manta added video projections. First, however, guests got packed off for a twenty-minute plod around Cologne’s municipal gardens. Talking was verboten. Instead, walkers were encouraged to listen deeply and perceive how their footfall intersected with noises from screeching parakeets, grumbling freight trains or crackling leaf litter. They then scribbled notes onto postcards and hung them on a display outside the church. Inside, Chisholm cradled his saxophone on a low stage in front of a set design where orange and purple light transformed sheets of foil into cragged ridges resembling a mountain face. The New Zealander had attached a feather from his homeland to his horn. He sat beside an accordion-like instrument called a shruti box. Traditional Māori wind instruments including kōauaus and pūtōrinos rested on his lap and hung around his neck. A dozen or so figures shuffled into a circle at the back of the church and started singing. The Ritual choir welcomes all volunteers, regardless of experience or music-reading ability. They kicked off the concert with a short, spectral composition by local musician Dariya Maminova. Chisholm added whistly calls while simultaneously coaxing a low-note drone from the shruti box with his right hand. For most of the concert, Chisholm cycled through his hardware to send sheets of sound swirling across the incense-scented interior of the church. Twice he chanted a Latin-language excerpt from Virgil's Georgics that referenced beekeeping. Nacken’s manipulated recordings of bee activity fizzed and bubbled, while Manta’s visuals swam from geometric patterns to clumps of crawling bee bodies. Chisholm descended from the stage towards the end of the evening and paced around the pentagon-shaped space playing buzzy, waggle-dance lines on his saxophone. His route took him past ceramic objects designed by Manta specifically for the occasion, as well as a small box containing a group of gently humming real-life bees from Hannah Liebig’s nearby apiary. Those footsteps recalled the earlier sound-walk, closing the distance between performer and audience. The event’s conceptual framework encouraged attendees to view the beehive as a world of sounds and images that represent key facets of collective life: Rigid physical and social structures, mutual dependence, and vulnerability in the face of environmental change. Strikingly, bees’ movements often appear chaotic—but hives are coherent places. Bees lean into their work. They embrace their rituals. They listen to each other. And that listening holds their world together. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: experimental / free improvisation / world music / sound art / drone
items._cn_summary: 这是一场在科隆Neu St. Alban教堂举行的跨学科仪式音乐会，新西兰萨克斯演奏家Hayden Chisholm与声音设计师Robert Nacken合作，将教堂内部转化为一座想象中的蜂巢。演出前观众被要求在市政花园中进行二十分钟的静默聆听散步，记录脚步与鹦鹉、火车、落叶的声音交汇，随后在教堂内参与合唱、聆听Chisholm演奏萨克斯、shruti盒以及毛利传统管乐器kōauau和pūtōrino。Nacken操控蜜蜂活动录音营造嗡鸣声场，视觉艺术家Natalia Manta提供几何图案与蜂群影像投影。Chisholm引用维吉尔《农事诗》中关于养蜂的拉丁文段落吟唱，演出尾声他走下舞台在五角形空间内游走演奏，使表演者与观众的距离消融。整场活动融合了田野录音、仪式合唱、电子处理与毛利传统乐器，体现了多层次感官体验与社区联结的深层思考。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / experimental / African traditional / global fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国-肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的Odd Okoddo二人组，联手83岁肯尼亚东部传统dodo歌唱传统的歌手Ogoya Nengo共同完成。Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打击乐与套鼓构成律动基底，与人声形成层次丰富的对话。评论以"Bara"为例，分析了合成器节奏如何从突兀逐步融入直至看似有机存在的过程；"Sarah"则展示了电子音效如何强化人声的情绪张力。文中将这类音乐归入"folktronica"范畴，并与Chouk Bwa、Nyege Nyege厂牌等探索性合作并置讨论，指出当代音乐的核心特征在于文化间真正相互回应而不践踏传统，根源可成前卫，创新也可显古老。这张专辑正是这种模糊边界的体现——三位音乐人的合作既植根于非洲本土传统，又通过电子手段与跨文化对话将其推向当代实验场域。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Milanese impressionistic prog/J-R Fusion band continues to grow and expand--this time in even more unpredictable directions! 1. "Oort Cloud" (6:21) etheric/ambient atmospherics open this one--a long, slow development as Fender Rhodes, heavily-distorted guitar, heavy bass notes and chords, and synthesized "bassoons," "flutes," and other atmospheric noises slowly populate and fill the sound scape. Amazing that this flute is not real (or else it would be credited, right?) Nice diversion but not quite what I was expecting and/or hoping for from this band's third album. (8.667/10)2. "Vogon" (4:51) smooth Jazz-Rock Fusion that is more in the realm of what I was expecting--add the bonus of an appearance of the great theatric cabaret Jazz artist Claudio Milano to sing/recite in his Demetrio Stratos way the lyrics to a made up language that the Aether gang created themselves (inspired by Douglas Adams' Hitchiker's Guide to the Universe). I love the music! It's quite like that of one of my favorite 21st Century bands, UNAKA PRONG, from North Carolina. Much more sophisticated than the gentle/soothing-yet-dominant Fender Rhodes would reveal. Very happy-go-lucky and up-lifting. (9.25/10)3. "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres" (8:42) ambient electric guitar picking in a sonicsphere of lush reverb is thickened by the joinder of layers of keys and bass before orchestral drums and electronic keyboard and lead guitar enter to jazzify the music as if Andy Summers and Robert Fripp were together again playing with an electronica keyboard wiz. In the fifth minute things quite down as Andrea Ferrari's guitar work begins to lead the band into a kind of SONAR-scape of Minimalist Math Rock. At 5:20 then we move into a more spacious scape in which Matteo's tom-tom pattern provides the foundational movement for a jazzy Fender Rhodes solo and, later, a weave with Andrea Grumelli's heavily-treated bass and Ferrari's distorted lead guitar in the mix. The heavily-reverbed song ends with the instruments slowly dismantling and slowing down the weave, reminding me a lot of 4 AD's 1980s instrumental band DIF JUZ. Nice piece. (18/20)4. "La Mélancolie Du Petit Prince" (4:37) over/within Andrea Serino's classical piano ruminations the other instrumentalists add their tracks of untreated fretless bass, computer glitch sounds, and natural and unnatural percussion sounds. It's as if Eric Satie was caught in a sombre-yet-romantic mood playing a piano in an empty French chateau while a group of construction workers and electricians were doing restoration work in and just outside other parts of the piano's salon or grand ballroom. (I can't stop picturing Chantilly.) Or one could compare this to Ruyichi Sakamoto's 21st Century (or life-long) fascination with sound recording glitches--the work he did with Christian Fennesz and/or Alva Noto. Pretty and suitably dystopian for our times. (9/10)5. "Panta Rei" (8:00) more (a different kind of) piano-founded sound exploration: it's not always harmonically pleasing, always on the edge of being melodic in familiar Western ways, on the edge of being satisfying while never really hitting the "right" notes. It's reminiscent of 1970s exploratory jazz (think Keith Jarrett) and also Smooth Jazz (Ahmad Jamal) yet also totally pleasing--at least, until the fifth minute when Serino and Grumelli lock into a five-note, three-chord progression to support Ferrari's rock-jazz guitar solo (that reminds me of John Abercrombie, Sonny Sharrock, Larry Coryell, and Fred Frith channeling their most aggressive Jimi Hendrix and Ornette Coleman energies). The song ends with Serino's piano, all alone, gently tucking us into bed. Interesting--to say the least. I really like a lot of it, though I've never been a serious fan of the free and loose distorted guitar shredding that Ferrari uses here. (13.5/15)6. "Swerve" (10:42) thought this song opens with simple, straightforward (almost child-like) Fender Rhodes play, other tracks of synthesizer and guitars soon join in, taking the music into more serious realms. Soon Ferrari seems to be relying predominantly on a heavily-treated (reverb) guitar sound--one that reminds me of Eef Albers on Focus Con Proby's "Wingless" and "Orion" as well as the "infinity" guitars of Michael Brook and Dif Juz. By the end of the fourth minute the song has become a serious Rock-infused Jazz of the 1970s variety, even incorporating time signature slow downs and speed ups, swaying shifts into more stereotypic Rock stylistics while and before re-incorporating more Jazz-expressive sounds, lines, and motifs. Matteo Ravelli's excellent drumming plays hugely throughout this one as does Ferrari's lead guitar while Grumelli and Serino's work provides more of the foundational work to keep this one on the rails. The final motif (presented in slow down mode) sees the blending and turn-taking of all four instruments before Ferrari's last notes sound, decay, and slowly fade away. (18/20)Total Time 43:13As a blend of old and new this album stands out as an excellent bridge--one that feels experimental and exploratory while, as alluded to, also firmly expressive, even honorific, of old "classics." This alone makes it a remarkable album but also the fact of the use of totally fresh and original compositions to do so makes it doubly so. Though it's hard for me to say that I like or love this music, I do find it fascinating and I do, very much, appreciate the labor and creativity that went into creating it. This has been a fun and enjoyable album to take my time getting to know but I don't know how much I'll be listening to it once the year passes. B+/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of genre- and stylistic-blending Jazz Fusion. The band continues to explore and progress and I commend them and urge them to continue doing so.
items._genre: post-rock / math rock / jazz fusion / ambient / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自米兰的印象派前卫融合乐队，以电钢琴、合成器与失真吉他为核心，通过缓慢的氛围铺陈构建出丰富的声场。第一曲以氛围电子和合成器模拟管乐开场，节奏悠缓；第二曲转向流畅爵士摇滚融合，引入戏剧化的声乐朗诵，灵感来自《银河系漫游指南》。第三曲将极简数学摇滚与电子键盘交织，吉他与低音在混响中编织，后半段趋于解构。第四曲以古典钢琴为基础，叠加无品贝斯与故障音效，形成萨蒂式的孤独美感，类似于坂本龙一与电子音乐人的合作质感。第五曲继续以钢琴为主导，探索不同质感的声响空间。整体融合了爵士摇滚、数学摇滚、氛围与电子元素，跨域整合能力强，富有实验精神。

items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - David Virelles: piano; Reggie Workman: bass; Andrew Cyrille: drums. Recorded at the legendary Van Gelder Studio, Creative Inspirations marks the debut album by Trio Imagination, which pairs the instantly recognizable Cuban pianist David Virelles with the unique rhythm team of bassist Reggie Workman and drummer Andrew Cyrille. These seasoned foundation builders invited Virelles to join them for a sort of spinoff of Trio 3, following saxophonist Oliver Lake's retirement from performing. Virelles' " Unseen Mother I " opens the album in an atmospheric, highly cinematic way, with punctuated piano constellations, wet percussion, and bright, piercing metallic sounds. Workman's fabulous woody bass arrives gallantly as Virelles expands the harmonic texture of the setting. " Unseen Mother II " reaches even more hypnotic realms. Both pieces derive from a nearly two-minute sketch included on the pianist's 2012 album Continuum , which happens to feature Cyrille. " Universal Sketches " places excellent bowed bass at the center, with Workman extracting exquisite overtones within a big, resonant sound. He then turns to pizzicato while the trio dives into obscurity and obliqueness. It's impossible not to fall in love with the trio's impeccable rendition of Andrew Hill's " Refuge ", which, despite being presented in a more straightforward way, acquires a fresh and personalized style via its demonstrative 6/8 time signature. Virelles plays it beautifully, and Cyrille enjoys a brief solo drum passage at the end. Among the best pleasures on the recording are the delightfully percussive, Afro-Caribbean-focused pieces such as " Pétalo ", " Neves ", and the closer " Para Ti ", which come full of timbral expertise and rhythmic elasticity. With angular structures creating an aura of incessant rhythmic discovery, these compositions amp the abstraction and curiosity with both transcendent foundations and noble, vivid harmonic surfaces. The piano groove in " Pétalo ", a piece composed by Virelles specifically for this trio, offers a grandiose Cuban feel, featuring an expressive bass solo followed by outgoing piano impulses. " Neves " continues this intelligent, modern approach, coming out with significant Latin vibrancy, imaginative polyrhythmic daring, and intuitive motivic insight, while " Para Ti " is a typical Virelles exploration charted with a conspicuous melody over a rattling rhythm. Trio Imagination moves freely from notated to spontaneous composition with genuine passion, effortlessly generating striking contrast in tonal color. Creative Inspirations is exactly what the title suggests—an album that leaves us wanting more as its curious layers and blends linger in our heads. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Pétalo ► 04 - Refuge ► 06 - Neves ► 07 - Para Ti

items.body: One of the hazards of reviewing drone and ambient albums is the overuse of words like expansive. And yes, Giulio Aldinucci‘s Materia is expansive. Glad I could clear that up. It is also luminous. Another overworked adjective. But I’ll come back to that. The title translates as “Matter,” and Aldinucci has spoken of sculpting the album by removing excess material from the sound mass. Listening to Materia, that image feels entirely appropriate. Every sound appears carefully weighed, every layer stripped back until only its essential behaviour remains. Nothing feels ornamental. The opening “Not Here” is also the album’s most articulated piece. It perfectly captures the tension between accumulation and subtraction that defines the entire record. As its most dynamic composition, it could easily have occupied the centre of the album as a climax. Instead, Aldinucci places it first. It feels almost as though he says everything he wanted to say in the opening eight minutes, freeing himself to concentrate thereafter on the journey without worrying about the destination. Harmonics continually oscillate between warmth and cold while, almost imperceptibly, a melodic contour begins to emerge from what initially resembles a shifting weather system of distorted drones. There is something unexpectedly romantic about it. Full of longing, even heartache. It made me think of someone who knows they are making love to their partner for the last time. “In A Shadow of Noise” immediately begins removing material. The music becomes less concerned with harmonic expansion than with the gradual redistribution of energy inside the sound field. Low frequencies acquire greater physical presence without ever becoming oppressive, while textures slowly roughen around the edges, allowing noise to behave almost like another harmonic component. The emotional centre of the album lies in the paired compositions “Cenere e Onde Lontane” [Ashes and Distant Waves] and “Come Luce, In Sogno” [Like Light, In a Dream]. Here the appearance of distant vocalisations quietly transforms the music. If I am allowed to use the word “spiritual” in a review of a drone record, this is where Materia becomes exactly that. The voices drift in and out of focus like fragments of memory, illuminating the album from within while introducing an unmistakable human warmth. The harmonic field suddenly feels more vertical, more open, as though the music had briefly lifted itself free from gravity. “Never” redirects the album once again. It is darker, denser and less organic, concentrating on texture more than harmonic bloom. Built upon a low, persistent hum, fine granular activity continually chisels away at the surrounding texture. The closing “Sera” [Evening] feels like the natural consequence of everything that precedes it. Harmonics soften, the modular textures become increasingly delicate, and a quiet melancholy gradually settles over the music. There is no final statement, simply the impression that the material has reached a point where nothing further needs to be added—or removed. And yes, Materia is expansive. More importantly, it glows from within. To expand on the materiality of his latest album, we reached out directly to Giulio Aldinucci. In your notes you describe Materia as shaping sound by “removing excess material from the sound mass,” almost like a sculptor working with stone. How did this idea develop, and did thinking of sound as physical matter fundamentally change the way you composed compared to previous albums such as Disappearing in a Mirror or Shards of Distant Times? Ever since Borders and Ruins, and especially on the two albums you mentioned, I have always worked from particularly dense, highly tactile sound masses created through granular synthesis, from which I then structured the compositions. This approach reached an even greater level of complexity in the works collected on Materia. On one side, there is an extremely rich, dense sonic material; on the other, the need to shape it using the appropriate tools. Editing therefore became an integral part of the compositional process through the use of extremely precise static and dynamic equalizers, allowing me to work directly on the harmonic content by smoothing or removing frequencies with surgical selectivity. The radical difference between the initially raw material and the final result achieved through this process of “removal” ultimately convinced me to give the album the title Materia. One of the most remarkable aspects of Materia is its treatment of time. Although the music unfolds slowly, it never feels static. The smallest spectral shifts, changes in density, and subtle rearrangements of microscopic sonic fragments continually reshape the listener’s perception of duration. In your accompanying text you write that “time can be matter too,” capable of being shattered into milliseconds and recomposed beyond conventional rhythm. Could you talk about how this idea operates in practice? At what point does editing become composition, and how do you know when a piece has reached its final form? The parallel with sculpture, deliberately obvious, helps me explain by contrast a second concept that is actually quite distant from it. Granular synthesis allows me to treat time as if it were a material to be moulded, working at the temporal scale of microsound. A sound is split into tiny fragments (grains) lasting between roughly one and one hundred milliseconds. These grains can be layered together and played back in a different temporal order, at different speeds, volumes, and pitches. The resulting masses of grains expand and contract like countless droplets within a cloud of vapour. To put it as simply as possible: from a single voice I can create the sound of a choir. It is an extremely complex technique and also the most radical form of sound processing, because it allows control over every aspect of sound, including time itself. A sound can be shattered into fragments only a few milliseconds long and then recomposed by reorganising those fragments into a different temporal order. Returning to the sculptural metaphor, precision equalizers represent the via di levare—the process of removing material—while the grains, these temporal fragments that accumulate into layered sonic masses, embody the via di porre, building through addition. A composition reaches its final form when I can hear within it the original idea that gave birth to it. Your work has long explored memory, place, and the dialogue between environmental recordings and electronic transformation, yet Materia feels unusually tactile. Rather than evoking specific locations, the album seems concerned with the physical behaviour of sound itself—its grain, weight, porosity, and internal movement. Do you see this album as marking a shift in your artistic concerns, or is it another way of approaching the same questions that have occupied your work for many years? Both perspectives are part of Materia. Everything grew out of ideas I have been developing over many years, yet at the same time I feel I pushed those reflections to their extreme, transforming them into something different. It is no coincidence that the compositions I am working on while answering this interview are very different, as though I no longer feel the need to add anything further to the discourse of Materia. Speaking about the starting point, I feel that memory and place are both very present in Materia. There are a few quarries around my hometown, and seeing marble blocks ready to be shipped has always been very familiar to me. All the fields around my home are the exact colour of raw sienna, the pigment known in Italy as “terra di Siena” (“earth of Siena”). When the fields are ploughed or the soil is wet, the colour becomes almost identical to burnt sienna. This landscape has therefore always been part of my visual memory. With this album I wanted to let the physicality of sound speak for itself, through a play of presence and absence; geometries in which the listener may also imagine what has been removed, or what might have happened had I removed even more. Across your discography there is an extraordinary attention to detail, yet your music never feels clinically constructed. Even the most heavily processed sounds retain an organic quality, as though they possess their own internal life. You have described the interplay between organic and synthetic sound as central to your practice, but listening to Materia I often found myself wondering where that distinction actually begins to disappear. Do you still think in terms of field recordings, instruments, and electronics as separate categories, or have they become simply different states of the same sonic material? This is a central aspect of my work, both aesthetically and philosophically. Although I no longer think of field recordings, instruments, and electronics as separate categories, the analysis of each individual component has become increasingly important in my practice. In other words, these are all sound sources that must be explored with great care, never taking for granted that I already know everything about them. This is an essential step that allows me to treat them as different states of the same sonic material, a description that resonates deeply with me. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: Giulio Aldinucci 的《Materia》以"物质"为题，通过削减声波质量中的多余材料来雕琢声响，每一层声音均经过精密称量，去除一切装饰性元素。开场曲"Not Here"成为全专辑最具动态张力的陈述，此后的曲目则专注于旅程本身。低频获得更强的物理存在感，纹理逐渐粗粝化，噪音几乎成为另一种泛音成分。中段两首作品引入远处的声乐片段，若隐若现如记忆碎片，为整张唱片注入难以忽视的人性温度，使音乐在垂直方向上短暂挣脱重力的束缚。终曲"Sera"作为前序发展的自然结果，泛音趋于柔和，模块化纹理愈发精致细腻。整张专辑在积累与减法之间维持着持续的张力，呈现出深沉的浪漫色彩与告别般的情感质地。

items.album: The SPKtR interview: Noise, Machines and the Refusal to Stand Still
items.excerpt: SPK have never made much sense as an argument for artistic consistency. items.body: SPK have never made much sense as an argument for artistic consistency. If anything, their history suggests the opposite: that continuity can reside in refusing to preserve a fixed sound, method or even definition of what a musical project is supposed to be. Graeme Revell’s current work as The SPKtR extends that principle into a very different technological environment, one in which artificial intelligence, algorithmic gatekeeping and increasingly unstable distinctions between human and machine production have become part of the artistic material itself. Our conversation began with the contrasting directions currently emerging around The SPKtR and the considerably more abrasive SPKtR XXX, but quickly expanded into something larger: post-humanism, seduction as a mechanism of control, the politics of technological systems, the usefulness of unpredictability, nostalgia, artistic failure and the boundary between music and noise. We also returned to the difficult Wave-Gotik-Treffen debut and looked ahead to November’s Wroclaw Industrial Festival, where Revell intends to present something very different: not a reconstruction of early SPK, but an attempt to recover its confrontational principle using contemporary means. The SPKtR interview Karo: The SPKtR now appears to be developing along two currents: The SPKtR, where melody, atmosphere and cinematic scale seem to have more room, and SPKtR XXX, where noise and rhythm become dominant again. I find that distinction fascinating because it suggests more than two versions of the same project. Are they two different ways of acting upon the listener – one through seduction and immersion, the other through physical impact and confrontation? What can one communicate that the other cannot? Graeme: You are absolutely right. It’s still quite early in my new period of creativity and I’m not sure what the parameters and boundaries of each project are yet. As a seasoned artist who has produced music in many different styles both for SPK and for film, I feel a little bit constrained by expectations. While ultimately I will move forward and produce music that I enjoy, I am aware of the audience that has supported me for decades and I am grateful to them. So I have recreated just a few songs, whose tracks were destroyed in a fire two years ago, to show my love, but I don’t think it comes as any surprise to say that the broader SPK project was ALWAYS about change and defying expectations. Most bands play it safe at later stages in their careers by rehashing their old material to nostalgic audiences, but I prefer to live dangerously and present new material that reflects contemporary means of production and issues. So, as you observe, these are two possible new versions of the project that reflect my love for both intense rhythm and noise on the one hand and melancholic and exotic melody on the other. Because they are extremes, it is difficult to jam them together, especially in a live concert context. But there are also other manifestations as yet unrecorded, and I wouldn’t say the project has bifurcated. Karo: “The Last of Men” deals with the erosion of human exceptionalism and our increasing entanglement with technological systems. That is an enormous philosophical proposition to place inside a piece of music. How do you prevent an idea of that scale from turning the music into an illustration of a thesis? Can rhythm, distortion, frequency or the treatment of the voice carry an argument about what a human being is more effectively than words can? Graeme: Another probing question. A four-minute song is never going to be able to deliver a coherent thesis on such a subject but, as with all my music, can act as a catalyst for somewhat deeper discussion outside of the music. My use of the term Information Overload as both a warning and a prescription for dealing with the social current of the late ’70s and early ’80s is a case in point. “The Last of Men” is similarly a warning and, as you say, simultaneously aims at a constructive argument against human hubris, which is central to our survival past the very near future. Quite a lot of my music I view as a post-industrial style of “protest song”. Going even further, the involvement of AI technology takes the project into the area of “post-humanism”, which I see not as the total removal of the human from the process, a la some of Cage’s modernist work for example, but as a decentring and a redefinition of our relationship with technology. I think the song can be an effective signpost for larger issues. Karo: “La Encantadora Furiosa” introduces a rather different temperature: something darker and more romantic. It made me wonder whether seduction might actually be as important to your current thinking as technological menace. We tend to imagine our relationship with machines through fear, but the systems that transform us most profoundly are often the ones we willingly desire. Is attraction, even intimacy, becoming part of the language of The SPKtR? Graeme: “La Encantadora” is certainly a different kind of song for me but does build on my years of film scoring, where I introduced a number of indigenous musical styles into film genres. From 1985’s “Zamia Lehmanni” I discovered my love of world music and very much enjoy exploring perhaps a different take. Sometimes a piece of music is just a piece of music, but I have always agreed that seduction, especially in late capitalism, is an infinitely more efficient system of “normalisation” and submission than naked control. This is something that I have spoken about since the very beginning as a disciple of Foucault. It manifests today in the continuous dopamine hit of scrolling and has become more or less a fait accompli. Karo: There is an almost absurdly perfect SPK story in what happened to “The Last of Men”: a piece written and performed by a human musician was removed from Bandcamp after an automated system apparently identified its audio as AI-generated. Early SPK examined institutions, psychiatry, media and systems of control; today some of that authority resides in platforms, recommendation systems and largely invisible algorithms. Did that incident change the way you think about where technological power now sits, particularly when the machine is no longer simply an artistic tool but a gatekeeper? Graeme: Yes, I did it as a test of the gatekeeping actually. There are, in fact, small elements of the track that are AI-generated and I wanted to find out how good AI was at recognising itself. Quite good, as it turns out. So the incident definitely didn’t change any of my expectations. I do, however, think it is absurd that the policing of the AI content fails to take into account that the content it is flagging actually owes its existence – partially but defensibly – to the very author, myself, which it has scraped. In other words, it has forbidden the creator to re-use his own IP. Now THAT is absurd. It is a very complex ecology of power but, as with any technology, provides new possibilities while foreclosing others. The role of the artist is to expose these relationships and hopefully to go some way towards subverting them. In this case, the task is twofold: to contribute to the database more extreme content that will exist towards the outside edges of the probability distribution, and to adopt a practice of multiple iteration that allows one to favour these extremes in creating new content. Karo: I would really like to ask about Wave-Gotik-Treffen because, from the outside, that performance seemed to acquire a drama of its own. It had been conceived as The SPKtR’s live debut with Robert, and then Robert became ill and could not perform. I also understand that at one point the show came very close to being cancelled altogether. Could you take us inside what actually happened that day, and how close you were to deciding that the performance simply could not go ahead? Graeme: Yes, it was a shock and I really wanted to cancel because I knew that I could only deliver half of a show. It was only when I was begged by many people who had promoted and paid for the concert that I agreed to do my best. Perhaps it was the wrong decision, but onwards and upwards. I was lucky to have the wonderful Evi Vine accompany me on two songs, but the robot technology I had been working on could not be deployed because I was nailed to the keyboard. Karo: What interests me beyond the circumstances is what that disruption revealed about The SPKtR itself. Did having to improvise around Robert’s absence expose possibilities that a technically perfect debut might not have? Is contingency still creatively useful in a project so dependent on technology and carefully constructed relationships between sound and image? Graeme: I have always been a solo writer. Even when Neil, the original co-founder of SPK, was alive, we worked entirely separately except on stage. So my shows are tightly controlled from my workstation. Robert is in fact the wildcard improviser, so that contingency was removed by his illness and the show was the lesser for it. The unpredictability is the fun thing about live performance and the robotic element is firmly still in this territory. We will see how it goes on tour! Karo: Wroclaw Industrial Festival appears to represent almost the opposite proposition: SPKtR XXX, harder and much more rhythmically and sonically aggressive. How different should somebody who witnessed WGT expect Wroclaw to be? Are we talking primarily about different material, or about a fundamentally different relationship between sound, technology, visuals and the audience? Graeme: The two shows will be very different indeed! I think there are only about four or five songs in common and I have radically remixed them. I am looking forward to WIF because I would like to re-establish the full-frontal assault that I think I began in 1978. There are one or two contemporary acts that have taken up the mantle but overall, I have been profoundly surprised how many of my contemporaries have not come up with anything new in the last three decades. In fact, there seems to be quite a lack of exploratory energy. With respect to the WIF set, I will try to deliver a visceral experience akin to how early SPK audiences described their reaction. The ubiquity of dark imagery nowadays means it is improbable to deliver the kind of visual shock that we once did, but sonically I think the experience is light-years ahead. It is a wonderful challenge! Karo: Wroclaw also comes with a very particular audience – people steeped in decades of industrial and experimental music. Does performing in that context create an expectation around the name SPK that you feel any responsibility to fulfil, or is frustrating that expectation still part of the point? Graeme: As I said earlier, I do feel some of that responsibility, but I also look forward to confronting their inevitable reactions, some of them no doubt critical, because throwing out different ideas is always the point. I always said that this variety of approaches was the essence of what has become lumped together under the term “industrial”. The difference is that SPK invokes this variety within a single show. I hope it’s exciting and fresh rather than frustrating. Karo: You and Robert have described yourselves, broadly speaking, as composer and instrumentalist, but by now the collaboration must have moved beyond such a clean division. What interests me more is where the two generations actually disagree. Does Robert ever hear something you have constructed and tell you that it sounds too recognisably like SPK, or that an instinct which once felt radical has become historical vocabulary? And when those disagreements happen, who tends to win? Graeme: As I have already stated, I am the sole writer apart from what Rob contributes on stage. So we definitely maintain a clean division. My work process is a very long one of self-criticism, which is why releases are few and far between. As such, there can be no disagreements. He is free to offer constructive criticism and I would listen for sure. But it’s unlikely that he would, because he understands that making mistakes is all part of the joy for me. And he has his own solo project. Karo: SPK has changed so radically across its history that perhaps its real continuity was never a particular sound at all, but an unwillingness to become fixed. With The SPKtR and SPKtR XXX now taking shape, what would constitute failure for you creatively? Would it be making something that alienates people, or would the greater failure be making something audiences immediately recognise, understand and comfortably identify as “SPK”? Graeme: Absolutely, it’s about discontinuity – finding and exploring different definitions of what constitutes the boundary between what is considered music and what is noise. I would like younger generations to enjoy the music I love to create. Failure to engage beyond the wonderful fans that I already have would constitute a kind of failure. Further, though, the “post-human” project is about shifting the appreciation of art from the old ingrained tendency towards aesthetic judgement to intelligent observation of the means of production. The incredibly rapid shift in the man-machine intellectual relationship – the means of production – is the crux issue of the day and is what my art is all about at the moment. This is not an easy shift for the listener. I revel in the danger that I might alienate people because if they allow that to happen then they do not really belong in this, our space. Yet there will always be nostalgia and conservatism, and I will tell you a funny anecdote to finish. I think it was our third ever gig in Sydney in 1979. At the first gig I had hidden one hand in my sleeve and was playing the synth with a large butcher’s hook tucked into it instead. After this third gig, an earnest young punk came up to me and said, “You guys were OK, but the band hasn’t been the same since The Claw left.” About SPK / The SPKtR SPK emerged in Sydney in 1978 around Graeme Revell and Neil Hill and became one of the formative projects associated with industrial music, although reducing their history to that category obscures how radically the project repeatedly changed its own vocabulary. Noise, extreme rhythmic experimentation, electronics, performance, increasingly melodic structures and eventually the atmospheric language heard on works such as “Zamia Lehmanni: Songs Of Byzantine Flowers” all appeared under the same name. That instability is important to understanding the present project: the relevant continuity is not one particular SPK sound, but an insistence that the project should remain capable of mutation. The contemporary The SPKtR brings Graeme Revell together onstage with his son Robert Revell. Graeme remains the principal composer, while Robert introduces the improvisational element that Revell describes as the “wildcard” within performances. The music is currently developing through several possible manifestations rather than one fixed successor to SPK. Broadly, The SPKtR allows more room for melody, atmosphere and the cinematic vocabulary Graeme developed during his long career as a film composer, while SPKtR XXX foregrounds rhythm, noise and considerably greater physical aggression. Revell is careful, however, not to define these as permanent boundaries; other forms remain possible and, in his words, the project has not simply “bifurcated”. That distinction will become particularly tangible during the forthcoming European dates. The tour begins on 7 November at Wroclaw Industrial Festival, where SPKtR XXX will present the harder configuration. Revell says only four or five pieces will overlap with the material heard at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, and even those have been radically remixed. His stated intention is not to reconstruct the SPK of the late 1970s, but to recover something of its “full-frontal assault” through contemporary production possibilities. items._cn_summary: 本文为Side-Line对Graeme Revell以The SPKtR名义进行的专访。Revell作为SPK的核心人物，其项目始终以拒绝固定声音和方法为原则，如今在新作中分化出两条创作脉络：The SPKtR偏向旋律、氛围与电影化铺陈，SPKtR XXX则回归噪音与节奏主导。访谈深入探讨了后人类主义、技术系统的政治性、不可预测性的价值、怀旧与艺术失败的关系，以及人与机器创作边界日益模糊的议题。Revell明确表示不愿通过重制旧作迎合怀旧受众，而是试图用当代技术与媒介重现SPK早期的对抗性原则。专访还回顾了Wave-Gotik-Treffen首演的困难经历，并展望了11月Wroclaw工业音乐节上以全新方式呈现的可能。

items.body: 第36回芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞選考演奏会 The 36th Competition of Yasushi Akutagawa Suntory Award for Music Composition 2026年8月30日 サントリーホール 2026/8/30 Suntory Hall Reiviewd by 齋藤俊夫(Toshio Saito) Photos by 飯田耕治／提供：サントリーホール <演奏> 指揮：阿部加奈子 新日本フィルハーモニー交響楽団 キーボード（石川作品）：秋山友貴、天野由唯 ソプラノ（中橋作品）：日野祐希 混声合唱（山本作品）：東京混声合唱団 エレクトロニクス（石川作品、中橋作品）：今井慎太郎 音響（石川作品、中橋作品）：片桐健順 <曲目> （第34回芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞受賞記念サントリー芸術財団委嘱作品） 石川健人：『嗅覚受容体』2台のキーボードとオーケストラのための(2026、世界初演) I.Aggressive! II.Fluidly （第36回芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞候補作品） 中橋祐紀：『And I sole ear（そして私はただ唯一の耳となる）』(2025) 金田望：2群のオーケストラのための『肌と布の遊び』(2024) 山本哲也：『戸外の鳥たちへのトリビュート』合唱と室内オーケストラのための(2025) 第36回芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞公開選考および表彰 選考委員：岸野末利加、桑原ゆう、佐藤聰明 司会：長木誠司   現在の現代音楽において最も問題・争点となるのは、調性如何ではなく、〈ポップであること如何〉だと筆者は見ている。ポップであることとは、必ずしもポピュラー音楽的要素を取り入れることではなく、現代音楽・前衛音楽がポップな形象を形作ることを是とするか否とするか、ということである。〈シリアス音楽〉という現代音楽の別名の語義とズレることを許すか許さないか、ということとも言える。 個人的な見解というか指向を述べさせていただければ、筆者は現代音楽がポップになることには大きな可能性があると見ている。西洋芸術（シリアス）音楽という西洋の民俗音楽の延長形としての現代音楽が、世界の音楽の多数派を占めているポピュラー音楽に吸収されていくことが現代音楽のポップ化であると捉えれば確かにそれは文化帝国主義的な事象であろう。だが、ポピュラー音楽を単一体として見るのではなく、多数の民俗音楽の複合体として見れば、現代音楽とポピュラー音楽は民俗音楽と民俗音楽の邂逅という可能性に満ちている。 あるいは、現代音楽が音楽的論理を突き抜けた先にポップな形を取らざるを得ないのであれば、それを〈シリアス〉という枷にはめて拒絶することはただの可能性の否定であり、時代に対する退行でしかないだろう。 枕が長くなったが、このように〈現代音楽〉と〈ポップさ〉についての考察をまず書かねばならなかったのは、本演奏会始まりの石川健人の委嘱新作『嗅覚受容体』の〈凄みのあるポップさ〉に当てられてしまったからである。第1楽章「Aggressive!」冒頭、キーボード2台がギクシャクとしたリズムでキャラキャラと光を放つ。その光がどんどん複雑に乱反射していくのに、次第に管弦楽が光点を押していく。キャラキャラと輝く音響はポップなのに、その甲高い笑い声は狂気すら感じさせ、恐ろしい。光を放つ各楽器の銘々が他の楽器の光を塗りつぶさないのは作品のエクリチュール、指揮者の采配、管弦楽団の技量ゆえであろう。キーボードとオーケストラがノイズ音を繰り返しクレッシェンドして第1楽章は了。 第2楽章「Fluidly」、弦楽器が透明な響きを広げるのにキーボードがジャラジャラと濁った音を撒き散らす。と、思っていたら弦楽器も奇っ怪、頓狂な音を放ち、キーボードは澄んだ音を発する。やがてキラキラしたエレクトロニクスと風か水のような弦楽器の中でキーボードと管楽器群が漂い、泳ぎ、蠢く。終盤、沢山のパートが時間差、音高差を伴って同型の上行パッセージを重ねまくり重ねまくり、音の物凄い飽和状態に至って、ゆっくりと各楽器の手数が少なくなっていって静かに収まっていき、さらに最弱音まで至って掻き消える。 オーケストラにキーボード、エレクトロニクスを加えての、輝かしいがギロリとした眼光炯々たる〈ポップさ〉、ここに芥川也寸志作曲賞受賞から改めて石川の音楽の未来を見ずにいられようか？ そして芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞選考演奏会であるが、〈ポップさ〉という観点からして、演奏された曲順から外れてまず金田望の作品を評したい。 『肌と布の遊び』、三宅一生の思想や仕事から着想を得たとのことだが、2群のオーケストラが衣、独奏ピアノが身体を表し、ピアノの可愛らしくさえあるフレーズに先導され、ピアノの周りに2群オーケストラがフワリ、フワリとたなびく。耳に聴こえるこの3者の音に加えて、3者のあいだの「空隙」に謎めいた音楽的感興がこみ上げる。ポップな触覚の音楽なれど、石川のギロリに対して、金田はフワリと、実に耳に優しく、心身を心地よく包んでくれる。筆者はファッションには皆目疎いが、こういうファッションは素敵だな、と素直に思った。 現代音楽における〈ポップさ〉とは離れた位置、言うなれば〈伝統的前衛現代音楽〉としてのアイデンティティを固持したのが中橋祐紀、山本哲也の作品であった。 しかし、〈伝統的前衛現代音楽〉という言葉を軽く使えるほど、この2人の音楽は易くない。 中橋祐紀『And I sole ear（そして私はただ唯一の耳となる）』、粘っこくおどろおどろしい弦楽器の上行グリッサンドに始まり……そこから楽想が完璧な連続曲線を描いて推移・展開していき、曲内の場面ごとの記述ができない。ウィーン表現主義が客観的構築性を極めることで主観的表現を可能にしたように、厳とした客観性を突き詰めた上で自らの主観に対峙し内攻する恐るべき現代音楽。ドストエフスキーの小説の登場人物の長大な台詞のように、果てること無く凄い求心力で筆者の魂を引きつけ続け、その力には文章で言う所の改行や改段落といった途切れがなかった。ソプラノ日野祐希の孤独な歌唱を味わいつつ、恐るべき音楽が書かれてしまったと愕然とした。 山本哲也『戸外の鳥たちへのトリビュート』、室内オーケストラの音による静寂が、音による自然を感じさせる。合唱も加わってのこの音楽による自然と我々人間との調和は確かに安らぎに満ちていた。ただ、静寂の中に浮かんだ筆者の耳には、その音楽に、いささか強めの言葉を使うならば、現代音楽的クリシェが潜んでいるとも感じた。この静寂と安らぎの中で今更〈新しいモノ〉を求めるのは野暮かもしれないが、筆者としては不満を抱いてしまったのは正直な感想だ。 プレイベントにも参加した疲れで選考会は遠慮して帰宅したが、選考会がとても熱かったと仄聞して惜しい気持ちだ。中橋祐紀の受賞は妥当だと思うが、他の2人が受賞しても不思議ではなかっただろう。現代音楽の可能性を確かめられた幸福な時間であった。 (2026/9/15)
items._cn_summary: 本乐评记述了第36回芥川也寸志サントリー作曲賞演奏会，涵盖三首作品。石川健人《嗅覚受容体》以双键盘、管弦乐与电子音响构建出华丽却带有凌厉目光的'ポップさ'，第一乐章'Aggressive!'闪烁嘈杂，第二乐章'Fluidly'在透明弦乐与浑浊键盘交织中走向极致饱和后消散。金田望《肌と布の遊び》受三宅一生启发，两群管弦乐如衣饰围绕钢琴形成的'空隙'中涌出音乐感兴，是一首触感温柔的作品。中桥祐纪《And I sole ear》以严密的客观构建逼近内省主观表达，弦乐粘稠上行滑奏与孤独女高音融为一体，连续展开如同长篇独白。山本哲也《戸外の鳥たちへのトリビュート》以合唱与室内管弦乐描绘自然静谧，但评论者感到其中潜藏着现代音乐的陈词滥调。乐评核心探讨了现代音乐中'ポップさ'的边界与可能性。

items.body: Julia Reidy’s intense, guitar-driven music blazes a trail along the less-travelled roads of the fretboard. Switching between a clear-as-day transparency and a wild tempest’s cluster of clashing and densely populated notes, her music is a constant surprise, bringing something medieval out of its withered and twisted shell and into the radiant light of a more experimental type of instrumental music. Beholder was born on the Greek island of Syros and came to completion in Tokyo and Berlin, where Reidy now resides. On Beholder (Room40), the Australian’s music stuns and hypnotizes, breathing out scorching plumes of fire and scooped speech balloons of black smoke, billowing out of the sound hole. Her guitar playing is, of course, a physical act – playing any instrument requires the use and willing submission of the body – but this physicality can actually be felt inside the music, the strings rattling with a sharp ferocity as they clang and scream on her opener, ‘Imminently’. The second track, ‘Syros’, has a completely different feel, beginning like a meditation with its manipulated chimes and its softer guitar repetitions. Although the tempo is quick, the rate of change is a slow, deep breath. Melding her guitar playing with a set of field recordings and electronics, Reidy’s instrumental music is unlike anything else out there, especially when so much of the guitar’s music is restricted to the first four frets. The guitar has an unlimited number of possibilities, so it seems a strange thing for so many to fall into a set of claustrophobic boxes and insular patterns. The musical capabilities are there, waiting for the musician to enter. Reidy is passionate about expanding the guitar’s tonal range. She is a channel: muscularity and physicality enter the music through her playing. She steps outside of the sound, which is less a disconnecting and more a gentle observing. This side-step, this trance-like distancing, actually brings her and her audience closer to the music. Echo-bubbles, trapped distortions and lacerating tones help to shape a vibrant and diverse world on ‘Jfai’, contrasting an unending guitar solo that would be thoroughly exhausting if it weren’t for the emerging bubbles of electronic sound, sending life-giving oxygen through the music’s veins. As a result, the guitar’s unceasing riffing is never in danger of suffocating the track, of blocking out the sunshine, and the four instrumental pieces burn brightly. The fifteen-minute closer and title track moves at light speed, too. Beholder’s strings clank together and weld deep friction burns with zen-like meditations. [bandcamp width=100% height=120 album=3530260669 size=large bgcol=ffffff linkcol=0687f5 tracklist=false artwork=small track=1620252459] Julia Reidy Room40

items._cn_summary: 朱莉娅·赖迪的专辑《Beholder》是一张以吉他为核心的实验性器乐作品，录制于希腊锡罗斯岛、东京与柏林。评论指出她的演奏突破了传统把位的限制，在清澈透明与密集猛烈之间自由切换，融合田野录音与电子处理，将吉他的物理性与冥想式的距离感并置。专辑中既有如开场曲般弦线震颤嘶鸣的激烈段落，也有以操控钟声与柔和重复构成的冥想式慢速变化；长篇器乐曲通过回响气泡与失真音色塑造出层次丰富的声音空间，避免了连续即兴独奏的疲惫感。整体呈现出对吉他音色边界的拓展意识与跨地域创作带来的开阔感。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在意大利Fazioli音乐厅录制的两小时即兴独奏，后经后期制作加入人声采样、打击乐、循环音效和实地录音。Sosa拒绝归类于任何风格，融合古巴音乐传统、自由爵士与电子元素，强调'无错误音符'与'少即是多'的哲学。专辑在新冠封锁与个人生活变动中诞生，旨在寻找精神归宿与人类共通的声音语言，以深沉的低频共振呼应传统吟唱。录音环境赋予琴声丰富的共鸣层次，混音处理保持简约克制，仅以稀疏点缀丰富原声即兴的核心。作品体现了一位艺术家在四十余年职业生涯中对自由的持续追求，以及对音乐工业分类逻辑的主动抵抗。

items.body: Childhood summers spent in Val D’Arzino made an undeniable impression on Davide Cedolin. The artist describes Friuli in northeast Italy as “Mountain people, feral animals, ancient trees, old crafts, lore, abandoned crashed cars, ghost towns, houses named as boroughs.” On Cjera Aʃìn, the artist performs a feat of alchemy by translating the memory, feeling and sound of the land into a luscious suite. The field recordings are crucial, plunging one into the heart of the remote area; the music fleshes out the narrative. At the very beginning of “Cedolins,” the cricket chorus declares its presence, making Cedolin the accompanist. His guitar work rests in the American Primitive style, warm and wooded, like a hike toward the shady glade portrayed on the cover. As the notes drop down, they do not intimidate; their function is to produce mystery rather than fear. The crickets continue to chirp at the end; this is their territory after all. “Poças,” the first of three long tracks, ups the ante with guest performances on hardy gurdy, shruti box, percussion and double bass. This time the first impression is created by soft rain and the call of a local bird; the piece develops into a thick drone, a mossy blanket of mood, the earth is sending notes through the loam. The players pull back to reveal Cedolin’s banjo, the rain still falling like the accumulation of years, reappearing in the next track with a slightly different timbre, like the memory of a different summer. This time cello colors the mist of memory, producing a wistful, melancholic tone. At some point we hear – or have already heard without recognizing – the artist playing “woods and bones.” The land creates its own music; Cedolin draws from its treasures to make more. The taps in “Cerdevol” could be bones; or the tapping of stones by the creek. The flow receives a generous allotment of time at the end, setting up the crackle of “Benaandants,” an extended work filled with accordion, synth and fire. Val D’Arzino is woven into the artist’s story as the artist’s story is woven into the woods. Echoes and reverberations populate the background of “Cjanâl,” but to the woods, the guitar is the more temporary sound. Warm, gentle narration introduces the final track, which at 12:18 is also the longest. Layer after layer rise to the surface, the artist exposing different facets to the light. In the sixth minute there arrives a softening, with leafy rustles, a slower pace and light percussion that swiftly dissipates to allow the notes to take center stage. The impression is like the region seen from afar, regarded in memory rather than in person, the scratching like notes on paper. In the tenth minute, the music disappears, leaving only scribbles of sound. One cannot pinpoint exactly when the album ends, just as one cannot trace the extent to which a memory can linger in the mind. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将意大利东北部弗留利地区的自然声景与记忆编织在一起。田野录音贯穿始终，蟋蟀声、雨声、鸟鸣与流水构成声音基底，吉他演奏采用美国原始派风格，温暖而木质。专辑邀请了手摇风琴、持续音盒、打击乐与低音提琴等乐手加入，在长篇幅曲目中构建出厚重的嗡鸣质感，如覆盖苔藓的毯子。班卓琴与大提琴为雾蒙蒙的记忆增添怀旧与忧郁色彩。手风琴、合成器与火焰声在末段铺陈出更深层的声响层次。最终曲长达十二分钟，乐层层层浮现，吉他音符逐渐消散，留下纸笔般的细微声响痕迹。整张专辑模糊了自然声响与器乐演奏之间的边界，将地域记忆转化为可聆听的听觉文献。

items.body: King Ayisoba Pure Confusion King Ayisoba's seventh album was cut live in a single sitting. Everything else was built around it afterwards Pure Confusion by King Ayisoba The most useful thing to know about Pure Confusion is how it was made. King Ayisoba flew to England in November 2024, sat down in Adrian Sherwood’s studio in Ramsgate, and played the whole record in one afternoon. He says the songs were already finished in his head. Nothing about his performance was altered after the fact. The bass, the cello, the saxophone, the harmonica, the dub processing on the desk: all of it was added later, to a recording of a man who was alone in a room with a two-string lute made from a calabash... items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是King Ayisoba的第七张录音室作品，其制作方式颇具特色：Ayisoba飞往英格兰，在Adrian Sherwood位于Ramsgate的工作室中，于一个下午独自完成了整张专辑的演奏，所有器乐部分——低音提琴、大提琴、萨克斯、口琴以及dub处理——均是在他原始的即兴演奏基础上叠加而成。他使用的乐器是一种由葫芦制成的两弦琴。专辑并非传统录音室逐轨打磨的产物，而是一次性的现场演奏为核心、后续构建其余层次的整体创作流程。Sherwood以dub制作闻名，为这张带有非洲传统色彩的作品注入了实验性的声音处理。乐评聚焦于制作过程本身，强调演奏的即时性与不可修改性，展示了世界音乐传统与dub实验美学之间的碰撞。

items.body: You won’t come back for me calling was an SOS one more stop for me one more stop for more There are songs about heartbreak that behave as though somebody ought to erect a marble statue afterward, and then there are songs like SOS, where Barcelona trio Low Blows seem more interested in the miserable logistics of having cared too much. You call. Nobody comes. You try again. Eventually affection begins to resemble a bad financial decision, and the sensible course of action appears to be locking your heart somewhere nobody can get at it, including yourself. That is a rotten way to live, of course, which is precisely why the song feels convincing. Carlos Vergara’s bass carries a lot of the burden here, moving with the blunt authority of somebody dragging furniture across an apartment at three in the morning. Rubén Carballo’s drumming keeps the floor firm beneath it, while Andrés Silgado’s guitar scratches at the perimeter, sometimes bright, sometimes abrasive, never hanging around merely to decorate the walls. The electronics slip through the gaps, giving SOS a slightly unreal temperature. The band’s industrial, darkwave, new wave, and shoegaze tendencies remain visible, though Low Blows sound increasingly comfortable letting those elements collide without stopping to announce which shelf each one came from. Vergara’s vocal delivery makes the emotional shutdown feel almost practical. Love has become excessive, softness carries consequences, and whatever emergency prompted the original cry for help has already curdled into weary acceptance. The final image of a heart shut inside a box sounds less like melodrama than somebody explaining the storage arrangements after the relationship has been cleared out. Carlos Vergara’s video gets considerably stranger. He takes public-domain footage from Stella Simon and Miklos Bandy’s 1927–28 film Hände: Das Leben und die Liebe eines Zärtlichen Geschlechts and drops its expressionist hands into Low Blows’ world. Fingers grasp, palms open, bodies overlap, and images of the trio pass beneath these enormous gestures from another era. Suddenly a nearly century-old experimental film has become an accomplice to a post-punk song made by three musicians scattered between Ibiza, Mataró, and Vitoria-Gasteiz. That accidental collaboration across ninety-nine years is wonderfully appropriate, as SOS revolves around reaching toward someone and discovering that the distance remains. Watch the video for SOS below: Since Cruel appeared in 2020, Low Blows have tightened their approach considerably. Go! brought producer Matteo Vallicelli of The Soft Moon into their orbit in 2024, followed by an OMBRA Festival appearance. Vallicelli returned for the trio’s new self-titled album, mastered by Maurizio Baggio at La Distilleria. Low Blows have found an ugly, elegant little groove in which emotional damage can dance without pretending it has recovered. Listen to SOS below and order the single here. items.album: Exploring the Swiss Label’s Catalogue Through Grauzone, mittageisen, The Vyllies, and More!

items.body: The history of mital-U begins well before there was a label to put on a record. In July 1979, Bruno Waser met members of the Lucerne band CRAZY at a Siouxsie and the Banshees concert in Baden. A year later, he produced CRAZY’s No Chance, regarded by mital-U and the Swisspunk archive as the first independently produced Swiss punk LP. The record preceded mital-U by sixteen years, but the encounter established the pattern that would eventually define the label: small-scale independence, personal relationships, and an interest in preserving culture that commercial institutions often overlook. Waser soon formed mittageisen, among Switzerland’s early German-language post-punk groups, combining guitar and bass with analogue synthesizers and drum machines. Their 1985 single automaten travelled considerably farther than their home country, receiving international radio play from John Peel. When mittageisen ended in 1986, Waser stepped away from the project, returning in the 1990s as mev2, or mittageisen version 2, where music became increasingly entangled with computers, animation, and moving images. Bruno W of mittageisen, 1983 That convergence supplied the foundation for mital-U. Its first website appeared in August 1995, at a moment when an independent music label having any substantial presence online was still unusual; the formal label and mital-u.ch domain followed in early 1996. Even its name carries several overlapping ideas. “mital” joins the German Mittag with “metal,” while the “U” can stand for You, Urban, or Underground. Over the next decade, mital-U issued mev2’s Geld-Arbeit, worked with former Grauzone member Marco Repetto, released Toini’s Electronic Biscuits, and participated in the Swiss Kult-Hits compilations, where Swiss punk and wave shared space with Yello, Kleenex/LiLiPUT, Grauzone, The Young Gods, and Stephan Eicher. By the late 2000s, however, another aspect of the label had become especially important: recovery. Between 2008 and 2013, mital-U released substantial remastered collections devoted to mittageisen, Grauzone, and the Lausanne trio The Vyllies. Master recordings were restored and digitized; photographs, booklets, unreleased material, and period videos were gathered alongside them. Waser has said that archival releases are undertaken with the bands’ approval, with trust and direct relationships treated as essential parts of the process. Across these projects, the catalogue offers several points of entry into Swiss punk, darkwave, and electronic music, each shaped by a different set of musicians and circumstances. CRAZY Lucerne’s CRAZY supplied the practical education behind Waser’s later label work. Formed in 1979, the group belonged to the first generation of Swiss punk bands, with a lineup that included vocalist Urs Knüsel, guitarist René Kaufmann, bassist Markus Tremp, and drummer Christoph Buri. In Waser’s account of the period, Swiss punk grew from frustration with bourgeois respectability and boredom, a local response to a movement whose methods could be adopted wherever people felt the need to make something happen themselves. The independently produced No Chance established that approach on record in July 1980. The later CRAZY (1980–1982) compilation gathers 18 remastered tracks drawn from the LP, the subsequent EP, and additional recordings, accompanied by a booklet. Its place in the catalogue gives the label’s post-punk history a concrete starting point: the bands, friendships, and self-organized releases that made the next developments possible. mittageisen Founded by Waser in 1981, mittageisen brought analogue synthesizers and programmed rhythm into contact with guitars, bass, and German-language vocals. Their self-titled debut, released in March 1983, helped establish the group within the early Swiss darkwave scene and earned Record of the Week recognition on the Swiss radio programme Sounds! The band’s name also carried a connection to John Heartfield’s antifascist photomontage and Siouxsie and the Banshees’ Mittageisen, extending Waser’s interest in the relationship between music, images, and political expression. By the January 1985 release of automaten / neues china, mittageisen had developed a more explicitly electronic, dance-oriented approach. The 1981–1986 Remastered collection, issued by mital-U in 2008, follows that development across 19 tracks, including six previously unreleased recordings, with a 24-page booklet. Further editions have kept individual parts of the catalogue in circulation, including the 2016 vinyl reissue of automaten / neues china and the five-track digital EP 1983 Remastered, released in 2024. mittageisen, 1982   Grauzone For many listeners, Grauzone will provide the most familiar introduction to mital-U’s archival work. The Bern group took shape in late 1979 around Martin Eicher, drummer Marco Repetto, and bassist G.T., with part-time contributions from Stephan Eicher and saxophonist Claudine Chirac contributing to performances and recording sessions. Eisbär, first recorded for the 1980 compilation Swiss Wave – The Album, brought the band international recognition, reaching the singles charts in Austria and Germany. Their brief existence nevertheless extended beyond that one song, encompassing material such as Raum, Moskau, and Film 2 before the group dissolved in 1982. Working with Off Course Records, mital-U restored and digitized recordings for 1980–1982 Remastered, released in 2010. The two-CD edition assembles 21 tracks and a 24-page booklet, including previously unreleased tracks such as the English-language Polar Bear and a live recording of Plastikherz. In 2011, mital-U also produced the first official video for Eisbär. Together, the collection and video place the familiar single within a fuller account of the musicians who made it.   Grauzone, 1980 The Vyllies Lausanne trio The Vyllies opened another part of Switzerland’s underground to international listeners. Ilona Prism, Ursula Nun, and Manue Moan met at the University of Lausanne in 1983 and began writing their own songs out of a shared concern about women’s place in the music business. Their first five-track release was recorded in Athens that December after an introduction through the Greek band Yell-O-Yell. Subsequent recordings brought cello, violin, and piano into their combination of synthesizers, bass, percussion, and vocals, giving their gothic and coldwave music a distinctive instrumental range. Across Velvet Tales, Lilith, and Sacred Games, the group developed a body of work that included Ahia, Whispers in the Shadow, and Now We Fall, before separating in 1988. Released in 2013, mital-U’s 1983–1988 Remastered gathers 29 tracks across two CDs, accompanied by a 24-page booklet. The label’s restoration work has also extended to Urs Egger’s video for Whispers in the Shadow, preserving the visual dimension of a band whose theatrical presentation was closely connected to its music. The Vyllies, 1985 mev2 and Toini Waser’s own mev2 project connects the label’s historical interests with continuing musical activity. Begun in 1994, eight years after mittageisen’s dissolution, it gave him a setting for further work with electronic music and video. The 1998 Geld-Arbeit releases brought Marco Repetto into the project as a remix collaborator, carrying a friendship from the Swiss punk years into techno and ambient music. That collaboration also informed Electronic Biscuits, released in 2002 and reissued digitally in 2022 as mev2 feat Toini. Raffaela Felder contributed voice, guitar, and electric piano, with Waser providing synthesizers and samples and Repetto joining him on remixes. More recently, mev2 has returned to mittageisen material through automaten (-6y edit) in 2023 and bestaendigkeit der erinnerung (v2) in 2025. These reinterpretations make the relationship between the label’s archive and its current work particularly direct: the same recordings can remain available in their original form while supplying material for new arrangements. Wire With Wire, mital-U’s interest in documenting post-punk extends into a feature film. The British group behind Pink Flag, Chairs Missing, and 154 is the subject of Wire – People in a Film, directed and produced by Malcolm Boyle and written by Graham Duff in collaboration with the band. Waser became involved through the project’s 2019 crowdfunding campaign and serves as senior executive producer, with mital-U working alongside Underground Head Films on production and promotion, including planned DVD and Blu-ray editions. The project draws on filming at Rockfield Studios and interviews with Colin Newman, Graham Lewis, Robert Grey, Bruce Gilbert, and Matthew Simms, examining the people and working methods behind Wire’s music. In a September 2025 update, the filmmakers outlined plans for screenings in 2026 to mark the band’s fiftieth anniversary, followed by a full release in 2027 for the fiftieth anniversary of Pink Flag. Those dates were presented as intentions, with the film still being completed. Material from the documentary has already appeared in Boyle’s video for 23 Years Too Late (24 Years Later Edit), unveiled in March 2026. The video accompanied the announcement of Read & Burn 03+, an expanded edition of Wire’s 2007 EP issued through the band’s own Pinkflag label for Record Store Day 2026. It offers an early look at the archival footage informing the film and connects that work to Wire’s continuing reassessment of its recorded catalogue. Beyond the Records Waser’s film work also includes an executive producer credit on Celeste Bell and Paul Sng’s Poly Styrene: I Am a Cliché, which premiered in 2021. Recent mev2 releases have also participated in EarthPercent fundraising, directing proceeds toward environmental causes. Now thirty years old, mital-U occupies an unusual position between label, archive, production house, and cultural workshop. Its catalogue moves backward and forward at once: restoring recordings from Swiss post-punk history while releasing new mev2 material, producing films and videos, maintaining an extensive online archive, and using revenue left after expenses and artist payments to support future projects or environmental and social causes. For Waser, preservation appears to be an active practice, requiring old material to remain available, contextualized, and capable of entering the present again. Follow mital-U: Website Instagram The post Celebrating 30 Years of mital-U — Exploring the Swiss Label’s Catalogue Through Grauzone, mittageisen, The Vyllies, and More! appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 本文聚焦瑞士独立厂牌mital-U成立三十年的历史脉络，以厂牌创始人Bruno Waser为核心，回溯其从1979年瑞士早期朋克场景起步，历经后朋克时期mittageisen的创作（吉他与贝斯结合模拟合成器与鼓机），再到1990年代mev2时期将音乐与计算机、动画、影像融合的演变过程。文中详细记述了厂牌与Grauzone、The Vyllies等乐队合作的唱片发行，以及2008至2013年间对历史录音进行母带修复、数字化与档案整理的工作。文章提供了瑞士地下音乐场景的一手史料视角，涵盖厂牌独立运营模式、艺术家直接信任关系及跨年代的声音探索脉络，但内容偏重历史叙述而非音乐本体分析。

items._cn_summary: 这是Carmen Villain的第五张专辑《Memoria》，与阿彼察邦·韦拉斯哈古2021年同名电影共享标题。专辑开篇以她上一张专辑中标志性的长笛音色在广阔混响空间中展开，但很快转入更为沉静的领域。整张作品拒绝轻松的聆听方式，要求听众放慢节奏、给予充分注意力才能感受其细节的绽放。相比2022年专辑《Only Love from Now On》中幽灵般、dub影响的朦胧质感，《Memoria》将这种语言推向了更深邃、更缓慢燃烧的境地。专辑聚焦于质感、空间与时间的延展，以极简手法构建沉浸式的聆听体验，适合愿意沉浸在声响纹理中的深度听众。

items.body: San Jacinto, up in the Montes de María on Colombia’s Caribbean side, had a dancer called Magdalena Ruiz. The gaiteros remembered her white smile and the grace in the way she moved, and how a gathering lifted the moment she arrived: the musicians, the dancers, the drinking, the young and the old. Adolfo Pacheco remembered her too: “Si no llegaba Magdalena, se enfriaba de la gaita el son”. If she failed to arrive, the gaitas went cold. “Ahora la evoco en mi cantar”, he sings, now I call her up in my song. Those gatherings take the shape of a rueda de cumbia. The musicians stand in the middle and the women dance around them, candles in hand, long skirts sweeping the ground. Caja and gaita set the pace and the circle follows. When Magdalena arrived, that circle opened for her. “Magdalena Ruiz” opens Madre Cumbia, the album Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto, Fruko and Carmelo Torres release on 20 October through the San Diego label Bad Vibes Good Friends. Ten songs, most of them from the sabanera repertoire: three by Andrés Landero, one Torres wrote himself, the rest from writers like Rafael Pérez and Betty Ochoa. Los Gaiteros have carried the gaitas of San Jacinto since the 1940s. Fruko was the bassist and producer who ran the golden era of Discos Fuentes. Carmelo Torres took the accordion straight from Andrés Landero, his teacher and the man who made cumbia sabanera. Between them they hold most of what happened to cumbia in the last eighty years, and this is the first time the three of them have been in a studio together. They recorded in Bogotá with nine musicians in the room, Rory Morison producing and Gabriel Torregrosa directing. On “Magdalena Ruiz” the melody belongs to Iván Salcedo‘s gaita corta, the short flute a San Jacinto cumbia is built on, and Carmelo Torres answers on accordion while Fruko holds the bass underneath. Behind them, caja, conga, guacharaca and maracas keep the rueda turning, and Rafael Castro sings the lead. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑《Madre Cumbia》汇聚了哥伦比亚加勒比海岸传统cumbia sabanera的三位关键人物：自1940年代起传承圣哈辛托gaita笛传统的Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto、Discos Fuentes黄金时代的贝斯手兼制作人Fruko，以及从cumbia sabanera奠基者Andrés Landero处习得手风琴技艺的Carmelo Torres，三人在录音室首次同台。曲目多取自sabanera曲目库，涵盖Andrés Landero、Rafael Pérez、Betty Ochoa等作者的作品。文中聚焦的单曲《Magdalena Ruiz》以Iván Salcedo的短笛gaita corta主导旋律，Carmelo Torres以手风琴呼应，Fruko的低音铺底，加上caja、conga、guacharaca和maracas维持rueda de cumbia的轮转节奏，Rafael Castro担任主唱。歌曲以诗意的歌词纪念圣哈辛托的舞者Magdalena Ruiz，讲述她的到来如何点燃聚会。整体制作在波哥大完成，由Rory Morison制作、Gabriel Torregrosa指挥，融合了哥伦比亚北部蒙特斯德玛丽亚地区的民俗传统与三位资深音乐人的演奏经验。
