items.body: Words by Justin TurfordThe iconic ‘Future Sounds of Jazz’ series has reached its sixteenth volume, an extraordinary achievement considering the Munich label Compost Records’ founder and compiler Michael Reinboth pretty much unveiled the term ‘future jazz’. This epic series of jazz-meets-electronica compilations began in 1995 and I’ve been a fan since the first edition when Michael drew the dots between artists as diverse as Luke Vibert, Patrick Pulsinger, Jimi Tenor and The Mighty Bop (alongside some lesser known names). A sonic space of jazz-infused house, breakbeats, future jazz and spaced out electronic oddities, the shared aesthetic was a jazz sensibility even if the music lived in other generic boxes. Not in a jazz sense of live improvisational musicianship but certainly in the sense of freedom, vibes, experimentation. From this early outing the world has caught up with Michael’s vision, a vision in turn inspired by Detroit’s own ‘Hi-Tech Jazz’, the Underground Resistance (Galaxy 2 Galaxy) all-time classic that revealed that jazz and electronic music could thrive together.Thirty one years after kickstarting this journey, the label returns with volume 16 and it’s another Michael (Rütten) who has been invited by his old friend to co-curate, and together they've absolutely smashed it, offering possibly my favourite volume so far with a roster that includes Momoko Gill, Trinidadian Deep, Felix Laband, Emanative & Jessica Lauren and DJ Oil.Michael Rütten is himself an essential cog in spreading the gospel about future-leaning jazz, electronic music and more. His globally-syndicated Soulsearching radio show has run for decades, he’s a music journalist, DJ and producer and has promoted key independent artists in his hometown of Frankfurt. Who better to join in the dig?I asked them a few questions on the eve of the release.. Michael Reinboth JT - Firstly, thank you for such a great compilation! Is it the best one yet? For my tastes it definitely is.Michael Reinboth - Many thanks for the compliments. Michael Rütten - Wow, that‘s a great compliment, thank you!JT - You’ve both been friends for so long and you’ve both curated many compilations but is this the first time you have compiled a record together?Michael Reinboth - Yes indeed, we’ve known each other since the beginning of Compost, and have a a genuine shared sense of taste, a journey through time.  After Vol. 15, I had a few good tracks up my sleeve but somehow not enough to fill a 3-LP / 2-CD set. That’s when Michael Rütten came along at just the right time. He had so many great suggestions that I was quite—and extremely—positively surprised, and I motivated myself to go into seclusion once again. Ha, I then found some rough FSOJ track listings on my old computer, gave them another listen, and sent my (old) ideas to Michael. Well, Michael Rütten really stepped up his game, so we currently have over 50 great tracks on our list and are already planning the next Vol. 17 for 2027.And we've decided to go on tour together and play this music in clubs, that is, to DJ. It's been a while since we've done that, and we think it's about time. Well, we're pretty good at it. After all, we have 40 years of experience.Michael Rütten - Yeah, and it happened almost by coincidence as we were talking on the phone earlier this year about potential compilations on Compost Records in the near future generally. I was relistening to some of the last ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ editions, especially Vol. 13 which Michael compiled on his own, for me one of the best ones, speaking about the selection, the flow, the feeling. All making sense. Also, I am thinking about a follow up of  ‘Soulsearching’ as it’s been quite a while. We speak on a regular basis about music, life, and what’s going on in the world of music and Compost Records. A new chapter of ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ has been ‘in the air’ since a couple of years, as not only there are so many new brilliant artists and tracks floating around that match with the idea of the series but also a new generation of young people discovering and appreciating this special sound of no boundaries, an open minded blend of jazz and electronics. I do feel and recognize this through my radio shows and DJ sets. So, as Michael mentioned that he could only think of two people - apart from himself - who could compile a FSOJ - one of them was me - we quite spontaneously decided to do the next edition together. Overnight we had a list of more than 50 tracks and started to sort (them) out. Which has been great fun! And apart from our dear friendship and shared love for good music I really do appreciate Michael’s attitude of ‘let’s do this’ and his open mind. And trust. As I do like his way of DJing ever since. Happy that someone just recently described us as pioneers of the DJ culture, instead of speaking of veterans ; ) We are still doing it out of pure passion. Neverending. So I am very much looking forward to travelling and sharing the decks again with Michael, spreading the music we love. Making people dance to timeless tunes of past, present, future via quite spontaneous DJ sets. No prepared set lists, always inspiring, always great fun also! JT - How did you approach the shared responsibility? Were there tracks that you had to fight over to be included or was it a relaxed process? Did you have fun?Michael Reinboth - First of all, it was a pleasure to hear each other's suggestions, it's always enriching. Then we basically gave the tracks grades, on a scale of one to three. No arguments at all. We were pretty much in complete agreement.Michael Rütten - Exciting, relaxed, open minded. Always enriching to hear each other’s new discoveries. And rediscoveries, tunes, that go a long way back and feel just right in the here and now. As we are both connected with so many artists of different genres from around the world who sent their music in and checking what’s going on daily or even 24/7 ... we both can’t just listen to everything. But tell each other about exciting new stuff. And I think it‘s a premiere that a fully analogue recorded jazz song made it onto Future Sounds Of Jazz - Brittany Davis’ ‘Sun & Moon’. Thanks to Michael’s open minded flexibility he instantly said yes to my idea. Oh, and no fights, never. FUN! Michael Rütten JT - When you started out with the idea of ‘Future Jazz’ 31 years ago (!), there were a lot less artists operating in that way but there seems to be a galaxy full of them now. Compost and the Future Jazz compilations have undoubtedly been leaders in the development and widespread awareness of the ‘scene’ - do you recognise that yourself and have a sense of pride in your essential contribution?Michael Reinboth - The term “Future Jazz” didn’t exist in 1994 (neither as a genre nor as a catchphrase among DJs), but I wanted to give this new stylistic phenomenon a powerful (and provocative) name. Basically, it meant: this isn’t acid jazz (i.e. old stuff or old stuff played anew) but electronically produced music, mostly created by recluses in the studio, as opposed to live bands. To answer your question about whether I have a sense of pride: yes, at the very least I can claim that, with the FSOJ series, I helped found and shape this genre.JT - You have both been at the forefront of exploring and revealing the links between electronic music and jazz for decades. What has changed in your opinion? Michael Reinboth - Back then, as mentioned above, it was mostly individuals producing jazzy electronic music; today, there are far more collectives (perhaps the first being Jazzanova) that can also perform it live (the Cinematic Orchestra, for example). It always takes time (much longer for jazz than for techno) for the tracks to become more complex and sophisticated - that is, to delve deeper into the essence of jazz, discover something new, and master electronic equipment and production techniques at the same level. But there were phases when Future Jazz was flooded by Neo Disco, New Wave revivals, Trap, Lo-Fi, and Broken Techno. That was also one reason why the intervals between FSOJ events grew longer. At this point, I have to once again give a big shout-out to Michael Rütten, who really helped me get back on track with it.Michael Rütten - Many projects, bands and producers that combine both worlds (jazz and electronics) have appeared on the scene over the last 10-15 years. Probably a lot of them inspired by the likes of Jason Swinscoe‘s Cinematic Orchestra, Theo Parrish, Nicolas Jaar, Matthew Herbert, just to name a few. Contrast Trio out of Frankfurt is one of them, just re-united with a new approach, or Momoko Gill out of London, who combines classic songwriting and live played drums by herself with jazz, soul and electronic elements. Emanative aka Nick Woodmansey also produces and plays music with the live aspect in mind from scratch. DJ Oil from Marseille/Paris with his quite unique sound. So much has happened and is still happening on the forefront of music which sits somewhere in between genres. I think that the pandemic has also played a huge role regarding this point. Artists had to find a new way of expression and took the time to either re-invent themselves or/and explore new territories. Jazz is the teacher, always or let‘s say again. JT - There’s a deep and hypnotic aesthetic running throughout the compilation (with a few exceptions). This cosmic-ambient-krauty-repetition way of composition is something I’ve noticed myself a lot recently on labels like We Jazz, International Anthem and many others. Do you think that this is the natural result of a generation of jazz (and jazz-curious) musicians growing up knowing and understanding electronic music? Is it also a sign of the times? A human need to explore slowness and transcendence in an ever-crazier world?Michael Reinboth - Oh yes, I do think that slowing down and a certain catharsis - escaping this crazy world - is a reason to turn to this music more than ever. It helps; it heals a little.Michael Rütten - Well, that is something I’ve just realized while doing the tracklist for the CD/digital release of FSOJ 16! And yes, it‘s definitely a sign of the times we are living in. And also all things go round in circles. With the overload of overproduced music plus AI most recently, producers, musicians and people feel the need to slow down, dive into soul-soothing repetitive moments, going back to the roots actually. Be it via ancient rhythms, ambient (healing) sounds, it’s soulsearching in the end. Seeking warmth and something to hold on to in this mad world. Electronic music evolved out of repetitive elements, exploring of sounds and a very free approach, far from limiting forms of music theory. Bringing the human aspect more into the creation. It’s a very exciting time period right now! JT - It’s been four years since the last Future Jazz compilation which had quite a different feel to this new one - What do you see NOW that could be a new direction in another four years in the future?Michael Reinboth - It’s completely trend-independent, but Michael and I have a few older tracks with a disco vibe—disco jazz, so to speak. Let’s see if we can put together a ‘Future Sounds of Disco Jazz’ compilation with them. For Vol. 19 or 20, I could imagine something more hardcore tech-jazz.I’m curious to see how our Future Sounds of Jazz DJ gigs go. The sound has been totally underground for years and I hope that will change in four years. We’re working on it.  Michael Rütten - Like Michael Reinboth said: trend-independent is the word here. Timelessness, always forward thinking without following any trends. Just following our instinct, gut and feeling. BUY HERE! https://compostrecords.bandcamp.com/album/future-sounds-of-jazz-vol-16

items._cn_summary: 本文是一篇围绕《Future Sounds of Jazz》第16卷合辑的对谈式乐评。Compost Records创始人Michael Reinboth与资深DJ/音乐记者Michael Rütten首次合作策划，延续了1995年开创的爵士与电子融合路线。文章追溯了该系列的历史渊源，提及Luke Vibert、Jimi Tenor等早期选曲者对'future jazz'美学的塑造，并指出其灵感来自底特律的Hi-Tech Jazz传统。新一辑选曲涵盖Momoko Gill、Trinidadian Deep、Felix Laband、Emanative & Jessica Lauren等横跨多国的艺人，呈现爵士质感与电子舞曲、碎拍、ambient元素的交汇。对谈还透露双方已为2027年的第17卷积累超过50首候选曲目，展现了这一独立厂牌合辑的持续生命力与策展深度。

items.body: There’s a whole mess of shows coming up in Vancouver, on bills featuring a fine mix of international acts and locals, some of whom we’ve seen before, and some new to our eyes. It’s a fine reminder that we’re living through a pretty healthy era for music under the umbrella of Our Thing, and while there’s no doubt a million things going on that are making touring very difficult (see Bragolin having to cancel all their US dates last week), we’re eating pretty good. Of course it’s not guaranteed to stay that way, so if you have the opportunity to go see some touring or local acts in your hometown, buy a ticket, grab some merch, try and keep the touring eco-system alive so we can all benefit from it. This pic is This pic is This pic is of Tronik (Youth) Datura Inoxia & Valanaïs, “Désir et Distance” Heavy, heavy TBM kicks and metallic programming run through the new collaborative EP from Datura Inoxia. Appearing on Ratflak, the same brutalist label which brought us the recent Blokkontroll LP, it’s a much rougher and more lo-fi version of the style the Mexican duo plies than that we associate with Berlin, but they’re drawing international producers into their grinding lockstep, including this gnarly looper done in concert with French producer Valanaïs. Datura Inoxia – Control-Represión by Datura Inoxia Wants, “Bitter Shape” Last year’s In Plain Sight was a real leap forward compositionally for Calgarian melodic new wave crooners Wants, and so we’re happy to get a sense of their next moves with a new single. Jeebs Nabil’s engrossing, winsome vocals smoothly weave through bouncy but spiky synth and guitar leads, with some raw Canadian anthemics bringing the likes of Spoons to mind. Bitter Shape by Wants Neuroticfish, “Eisbär” Neuroticfish covering Grauzone? Hell fuckin’ yeah. We’re unapologetic fans of both projects, and hearing the strong pop instincts of Neuroticfish meet the classic NDW sound of “Eisbär” is lovely. The track is taken from a compilation benefiting The White Rose Foundation, who do important educational work regarding the dangers of fascism, and our responsibility to pushing back against it. The compilation hits the streets November 6th and also features covers of welle classics from (*deep breath*) Stabbing Westward, Caustic, Leæther Strip, Nouvelle Vague, Modern English, EMF (!), The Dead Milkmen (!!), and John Fucking Carpenter (!!!). We Will Not Be Silent / Wir Schweigen Nicht – A White Rose / Weiße Rose Benefit by Neuroticfish Tronik Youth, “Touch Me, I’m Sick” Okay fine, so the italo-body music thing never quite took off the way we were hoping, it seems just as the whole thing was really starting to cook, many of the major producers veered off into NRG and other revivalist dance styles, which has a sort of historic symmetry to it at least. With that said, you still get some bangers that inhabit that not-quite new beat sound, like say this new one from London’s Tronik Youth, which has all the gnarly, mechanized funk and ominours textures you could want, while still being a righteous dancefloor heater. Touch Me I'm Sick by Tronik Youth Unconscious, “Tutto è una copia” There’s solid and unpretentious dark electro/EBM to be found on the latest single on X-IMG from the always impossible to google Italian producer Unconscious. The throwback production and slowly filtering pads feel like a nice mix of Xorcist and any number of Carpenter scores you might care to name. Also, check the B-side if you’re as much of a fan of Jesse “The Body” Ventura’s conspiracy rhetoric as we are. Cold Hearts by Unconscious Stuka, “Travelling Across Obscure Dimensions” Holy shit, what the hell is this? Best description we can come up with is baroque synthpunk about Warhammer 40k, but even that doesn’t quite encapsulate things. You’ve got the dungeon synth style medieval arrangement, and bellowed/screeched vocals paired with traditional folk singing. Even as total Games Workshop dilletantes, we have some working knowledge of the Imperium’s vast lore, but not enough to decypher this madness. Just a blast of unexpected weirdness, in the best way. Travelling Across Obscure Dimensions by STUKA The post Tracks: September 14th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于暗潮与电子舞曲领域的近期作品与演出信息。开篇讨论了温哥华即将到来的演出阵容，强调支持巡演生态的重要性。随后详细评介了四张作品：墨西哥双人组Datura Inoxia与法国制作人Valanaïs合作的EP，展现了粗粝的低保真TBM风格与金属化编程；加拿大卡尔加里乐队Wants的新单曲延续了旋律新浪潮路线，合成器与吉他编织出富有感染力的旋律线；德国电子乐队Neuroticfish翻唱了Grauzone经典NDW曲目Eisbär，作品收录于一张反法西斯主题合辑；Tronik Youth翻唱了Mudhoney的Touch Me, I'm Sick，延续了意式Body Music的美学。文章最后还列出了合辑中其他翻唱阵容，包括Stabbing Westward、Leæther Strip、John Carpenter等横跨多代的暗潮与工业艺人。整体内容侧重于小厂牌发行的暗潮/EBM场景，具有较强的地下属性。

items.body: 〈過剰〉を〈過剰〉のままで―沖澤のどか／SKOの《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》｜内野 儀 Excess in All Its Excess: Nodoka Okisawa and the SKO’s Turangalîla-Symphonie 2026年8月23日 キッセイ文化ホール（長野県松本文化会館） セイジ・オザワ 松本フェスティバル オーケストラ コンサート Aプログラム（2日目） 2026/8/23 Kissei Culture Hall (Nagano Prefecture Matsumoto Culture Hall) 2026 Seiji Ozawa Matsumoto Festival: Orchestral Concert — Program A (Day 2) Reviewed by 内野 儀(UCHINO, Tadashi) Photos by 山田毅(Takeshi Yamada)／2026OMF :大窪道治 （Michiharu Okubo）／2026OMF 〈演奏〉 指揮：沖澤のどか ピアノ：務川慧悟 オンド・マルトノ：原田節 管弦楽：サイトウ・キネン・オーケストラ 〈曲目〉 オリヴィエ・メシアン《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》 ©山田毅／2026OMF 《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》は、あらゆる意味で〈過剰〉な作品である。85分、10楽章、100人を超える大編成オーケストラ。独奏ピアノとオンド・マルトノ、数多くの打楽器奏者、そしてピアノ・チェレスタ・鍵盤グロッケンシュピール・ヴィブラフォンからなる「ガムラン」群。ティンパニもハープもない代わりに、これだけのものが投入されている。 〈過剰〉は規模にとどまらない。メシアン自身、第1楽章の中間部を「ポリリズム、ポリモダリティ、ポリミュージック」と呼んだ(1)第4楽章の再現部については、スケルツォ主題、ピアノ独奏、コントラバスのピツィカート、ガムラン群、リズム・ペダルを奏するウッドブロック、小トルコ・シンバル、小太鼓のリズム、木管とホルンの第1トリオ、弦の第2トリオ、そしてトロンボーンの第一循環主題（〈彫像の主題〉）——10の独立した音楽が同時に鳴ると自ら数え上げている（Messiaen, p. 227; Shenton, p. 49）。したがって、打楽器奏者には「第六感」をもちあわせた第一級の精度が必要で、小さな誤りひとつで音楽が壊れる、と書き残している（p.156; p.15）。 メシアンはまた、「歓びの讃歌(hymn to joy)」と本作を形容するが、その「歓び」の定義そのものが〈過剰〉である。「17世紀の実直なブルジョワ市民が味わうような穏やかで満ち足りた歓びではない」と否定形からその定義を始め、「不幸のただなかにあってかろうじて垣間見た者だけが思い描きうるもの、超人的で、溢れ出し、目を眩ませ、過剰なものだ」と書く（p.151; p.6）。「愛」についても、「トリスタンとイゾルデの媚薬によって象徴されるような、すべてを超え、自らの外にあるすべてを消し去る宿命的で抗いがたい愛」であるとする（同上）。この「愛」が、媚薬による絶対的／超越的「愛」である以上、そこに暴力性が畳み込まれているのは当然である。実際、冒頭でトロンボーンが重い3度で叩きつける第一循環主題を、メシアンは〈彫像の主題〉と呼び、メキシコの記念建造物の恐るべき残酷さを喚起するものと説明している(2)。要するに、この作品において〈過剰〉は方法や結果ではない。〈過剰〉こそが主題である。 そのことを考えるとき、私はどうしても作曲年代のことを思う。1945年6月25日、セルゲイ・クーセヴィツキーがメシアンに委嘱状を書いた。ドイツ降伏の7週間後である。メシアンの返信は8月20日、《ハラウィ(Harawi)》を書き上げつつあったプティシェ(Petichet)のサマーホームからで、「美しく、相応の規模をもった作品を書きたい。そのためには夢み、愛し、練り上げ、急がずに管弦楽化する時間が要る」だった(3)。 ソプラノとピアノのための連作歌曲《ハラウィ》(1945）、この《トゥランガリーラ交響曲》（1946–48）、無伴奏12声のための《5つのルシャン》（1948）。のちにトリスタン三部作と呼ばれる三作は、この数年のうちに続けて書かれた。編成も規模もまったく異なるが、いずれも愛と死をめぐる同じ主題系のもとにある。メシアンの作品のなかで、カトリック信仰を直接の主題としない数少ない例でもある。 同じ1945年の秋、メシアンにはもうひとつ差し迫った委嘱があった。アンリ・バロー(Henry Barraud)からの、戦時中の強制移送者を追悼する作品である。11月2日の演奏会に向けて、9月22日——《ハラウィ)》完成の1週間後——に楽譜を渡せるように《強制移送者たちの歌（Chant des déportés）》を書き、さらに、10月10日の日記には、「クーセヴィツキーのために交響的作品を書く」と記している(4)。 戦時中の強制移送者を追悼する作品と、この巨大な交響曲の初期的構想とは、同じ数週間のなかにあった。作曲そのものは1946年7月17日から1948年11月29日まで(p.151; p.4)行われたが、作曲者自身についても、よく知られているように、自らが収監されていたゲルリッツの捕虜収容所で《世の終わりのための四重奏曲》を1941年に書いて演奏もしている(5)。 1945年5月16日——ドイツ降伏の8日後——にメシアンが雑誌『ヴォロンテ(Volontés)』へ寄せた文章がある。「現代音楽には乾いた非人間的なものが多すぎる！」とかれは書く。「来たるべき革新者は言語だけの革命家であってはならない。絶望の塊や、人の住まない惑星ではなく、大文字の愛を」。そして、待ち望まれている「解放者」、すなわち「愛の作曲家」の到来をともに祈ってくれと呼びかけている(6)。「絶望の塊」。「人の住まない惑星」。「解放者」。1945年5月のヨーロッパで書かれた語彙である。 この交響曲が戦争を描いていると言いたいのではない。標題にも、作曲者の膨大な自己解説のどこにも、そんなことは書かれていない。だが、これほどの規模の肯定が何に対する応答だったのかを問わずに済ませることもできないのではないか。「不幸のただなかで垣間見た者だけが思い描きうる歓び」——この条件節に、1946年のヨーロッパで指示対象がなかったとは、私には考えにくい。廃墟の記憶は、フランスが戦勝国であったからといって消えるようなものではない。 専門家ではないので見落としが多いことだろうが、短期間ではあるものの目を通すことができた英語文献にかぎると、メシアンと戦争をめぐる議論は《四重奏曲》と占領期に集中しているようで、トリスタン三部作のほうは、もっぱら二つの方向に読まれてきた印象が残る。ひとつは本作についてのシュルレアリスム的プログラムの解読、もうひとつは作曲者の私生活——病んでゆく最初の妻クレール・デルボスと、イヴォンヌ・ロリオとの関係——への還元である。 後者は、私にはあまり実りがあるとは思えない。第一に、メシアン自身が私生活と作品を明示的に結びつけていない。シェントンも、まさにその理由でその論点を扱わないと断っている(7)。第二に、そもそも個人的な恋愛の高揚だけでは、この規模と構造を説明しきれない。この規模は、私的な感情の器としては明らかに大きすぎる。 もちろん、〈過剰〉は、説明されるべき欠陥ではない。これは端的に誇大妄想である。あるいは、過大妄想とでもいうべきか。初演前のNBCの放送でクーセヴィツキーは、《春の祭典》に次ぐ今世紀最大の作品だと言い切った(8)。誇大／過大な言い方である。だが誇大／過大であることこそが、この作品の内容なのだと思う。廃墟のあとに、この規模で〈愛〉と〈歓び〉を主張すること。〈まっとう〉な振る舞いではない。そして、〈まっとう〉ではないことが必要だったのではないか。 メシアンは1953年、自分は神秘主義の音楽家ではなくシュルレアリストの音楽家である、ただしその超現実への欲望は超自然によって超えられている、と述べている(9)。シェントンはこの発言を、ブルトンの『シュルレアリスム第二宣言』（1930）に重ねている。ブルトンがそこで求めたのは、「生と死、現実と想像、過去と未来、伝達可能性と伝達不可能性、高と低がもはや矛盾として知覚されなくなるような精神の一点」(10)であった。第一次大戦後に成立したシュルレアリスムの論理が、戦後期のメシアンの自己規定に重ねられる。歓びと恐怖を対立させないこと、〈愛の主題〉と〈彫像の主題〉とを同じ作品に置くこと。それは意匠ではなく、あの時代への応答となる思想として、私には聴こえる。 だから、この作品を単一の陶酔へ向かって収束させる聴き方には、私は与しない。緩徐楽章の〈愛の主題〉に匂い立つような官能を求め、終曲に忘我を求める——そうした期待は、作品の多層性を単一の陶酔へ狭める読みだと思う。 サンスクリットの題、ヒンドゥーのターラ、ガムラン、メキシコの記念建造物、ボスとシャガールとピラネージ。快楽の園と出口のない牢獄。この作品が抱え込んでいるものは、どこまでも多元的であり、その多元性には〈地獄的なもの〉まで含まれている。二元論を拒むこと、一つの中心へ回収されないこと。それが、この〈過剰〉の設計思想である。 ©大窪道治／2026OMF 23日の演奏は、まさにそれを鳴らした。沖澤のどかはこの日、指揮棒を持たずに振った。打点を棒で叩き込まない身ぶりが奏者に過剰な圧をかけず、テンポは「押される」のではなく「走り出す」。第5楽章や終曲の疾走感は、絶対的なテンポの速さからではなく、その場その場の奏者との呼吸から生まれてくる。〈自然体〉、という言い方がふさわしい。 そしてこの〈自然体〉は、〈過剰〉を手なずけるための方便ではなかった。同時多発は同時多発のまま残り、しかしカオスにはならない。第2楽章冒頭で三つの群が別々のリズムを刻む箇所も、ガムラン群が主要主題と併走する箇所も、均されることなく、それぞれの層として聴こえてくる。沖澤は公演前に、「すべてをクリアにすることによって濃厚にしたい」と語っていた。「どこまでも緻密に作ったうえで、それを体に沁み込ませる。そして、オーケストラが曲を知り尽くした状態にしたうえで本番に自由になるような——そこを目指」す、とも(11)。明晰さは削減ではない。〈過剰〉が混濁ではなく〈過剰〉として聴こえるための、重要な条件の一つである。抑制でも整理でもなく、〈過剰〉を〈過剰〉のまま、リアルタイムに立ち上げること。この作品にこれほど相応しい方法があるだろうか。 その姿勢が最も明瞭に出たのが、第8楽章の終わりである。「愛の展開」と題されたこの楽章では、〈和音の主題〉がよく聞こえる。だがこの楽章は〈彫像の主題〉で閉じられる。しかもその最後の音は、管楽器から、タムタム、大太鼓、ピアノ、コントラバスへと受け渡される。打たれた瞬間から消えはじめる音である。「愛の展開」が行き着いた先に、この落下がある。減衰を聴きつづけるあいだ、それが恐ろしいのか美しいのかは判別できない。沖澤はその減衰を、かなりの長さにわたって聴かせた。急ぐ理由がないから急がない。それだけのことが、この作品ではほとんど過激に響く。他方、全曲を締める終曲の最後は、極端に引き延ばされることなく、比較的速いポイントですっきりと切り上げられた。 四つの循環主題のうち、メシアンが唯一象徴的意味を与えなかったのが〈和音の主題〉である。かれはこれを、主題というよりも異なる音の層を成り立たせるための口実だと言い、中世錬金術の標語を引いている——分離し、そして凝固させよ。要素へと分解し、新たな形へ組み直す(12)。この日の演奏が全曲にわたっておこなっていたのは、まさにその作業だった。 ©山田毅／2026OMF 務川慧悟のピアノは、第1楽章のカデンツァから第5楽章の強打まで、和音の一音一音が分離して聴こえる明晰さを保った。強奏でも音が濁らない。舞台前方下手側にピアノ、チェレスタ、鍵盤グロッケンシュピール、ヴィブラフォン、上手側にオンド・マルトノという配置で、鍵盤・打楽器群の合奏はきわめて緊密だった。原田節のオンド・マルトノは、前から13列目やや下手寄りという私の席では音量的に前に出てこず、弦との溶け合いのなかに沈む場面が多かった。席位置による部分が大きいだろう。 緩急の振幅も、極大から極小まで振り切ったダイナミクスの幅も、「楽譜どおり」と言ってしまえばそれまでかもしれない。だが今回聴こえたのは、楽譜の指示の「再現」ではなく「現実化」だった。書かれていることが、その場で実際に起きるのだ。 私には、廃墟の記憶のうえに立つ〈まっとう〉ではない規模の肯定として聴こえた。それは一つの答えに収束することを拒み、多元的なまま、〈過剰〉なまま鳴りつづけるように感じられた。きな臭さを増していく2026年の日本で、その〈過剰〉が整理も馴致もされずに響いたことには、意味があると思う。純粋な音楽として、である。 （2026/9/15) 註 (1)Messiaen, O. (1995). Traité de rythme, de couleur, et d’ornithologie. Volume 2, Paris: Alphonse Leduc, p.163. Shenton, Andrew. Olivier Messiaen’s Turangalîla-symphonie (Elements in Music since 1945) , London: Cambridge UP, 2023, p.41からの孫引き。上掲書からの引用はシェントンの著作による。和訳はシェントン本の英語からの拙訳。以下、同書からの引用については、両書の頁数のみを記す。 (2) Quoted in Shenton, p.36. (3)ナイジェル・シメオン(Nigel Simeone)によるハイペリオンCDA67816ライナーノート(2012)の記述による。https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W14114_67816。シェントンもまた、シメオンの記述を引用している（p.4）。 (4)Ibid. (5)《世の終わりのための四重奏曲》についての、メシアンが収監されていた捕虜収容所での演奏や解放後の同曲の経緯については、Leslie A. Sprout, “Messiaen, Jolivet, and the Soldier–Composers of Wartime France”, The Musical Quarterly 87, no. 2 (2004): pp. 259–304に詳しい。 (6) Quoted in Shenton, p.21. (7)Shenton, p.35. (11)「 J-WAVE NEWS」2026年7月28日(https://news.j-wave.co.jp/2026/07/content-5509.html)。 (12) Shenton, p.38.シェントンが本書で引用するメシアン自身による循環主題についての説明は、1991年のドイツグラモフォン版の録音に付されたライナーノートによる。 [Performers] Conductor: Nodoka Okisawa Piano: Keigo Mukawa Ondes Martenot: Takashi Harada Orchestra: Saito Kinen Orchestra [Program] Olivier Messiaen: Turangalîla-Symphonie
items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦于梅西安《图伦加利拉交响曲》的演出解读，围绕'过剩'这一核心命题展开。评论者冲泽的どか指挥�的site�的乐团演绎，从作品规模、复节奏、复调性等多重维度切入，剖析梅西安对'喜悦'与'爱'的超越性定义。文章进一步将创作置于1945-48年战后欧洲语境中，探讨作曲家在战争阴影下对人性与希望的追问。文本引用大量原始文献与作曲家自述，兼具音乐分析与历史批评深度，对当代古典音乐爱好者及梅西安研究者具有参考价值。

items.excerpt: 米ミシシッピ出身で東京在住のディープ・ハウサーによるライフワーク・シリーズ第5弾。〈アンチAI〉をテーマにピアノやシンセ、リズムマシーンなど、すべてハードウェアのみで制作され、文字通り長尺のハウス・トラック6つで構成されている。削ぎ落とされた無機質な電子音のなかに有機的な柔らかさや温もりが感じられ、アトモスフェリックでドリーミーな聴後感が印象的だ。

items._cn_summary: 这是常驻东京的美国制作人威尔·朗的系列专辑第五作，以反对人工智能为核心创作理念，所有声音均来自钢琴、合成器与节奏机等硬件设备，刻意规避软件与算法介入。专辑收录六首长篇曲目，通过极简的无机质电子音色构建出柔软温暖的氛围感，冷暖之间的张力成为贯穿始终的听觉线索。作品呈现出梦幻而带有漂浮感的整体气质，在严格限制制作手段的前提下探索声音的有机表达，长篇编排为氛围的缓慢铺陈留出充足空间，使听感具有冥想式的沉浸特质。

items.body: Rauelsson’s driving beats slink through the after-hours, coasting through a neon-lit cityscape that’s been daubed in bright makeup. Fit for a night drive, the bleary-eyed music gazes out upon blurred electronic lighting and dim shop windows, its streets are like deserted ghost-towns, and a tiring melody skittles along a predetermined route at the speed of a night bus. Halogen lights bring a dark-jazz-influenced clarinet into the spotlight, illuminating its slithering, seductive-but-never-sleazy melody. This sophomore (to be released on Sonic Pieces) is a continuous set, featuring organic, driven beats, dark, phantom electronics, and a wide array of acoustic instrumentation. As is standard for sequels, the music on Mirall has expanded, grown, evolved. Sequels get a bad rep, but this isn’t more of the same, nor does it go past the same streets. If it attempted to copy and paste Rauelsson’s original (and successful) blueprint, the music would only suffer. Besides, it’s completely natural for the music – and the artist – to keep on growing and to flirt with new ideas, taking up residency in differing nooks. Mirall is at one with the night-owned shadows, vampiric in its preference for a night-drenched secrecy over the full, naked exposure of daylight. A piano will emerge, but even this is obscured by a rain-soaked crackling and a sleepy clarinet. The sedatives sit well with the more electronically-minded segments – the beats drive on, but they move at an easy speed, never hammering the throttle but instead making the transition to piano or clarinet a smooth one thanks to the cruising tempo. No gear change is required. The strings of ‘Mistral’ provide a moment of relief and something close to transient joy: a moment where dawn awakens and the white light begins to shine into the room. Slowly, the track begins to wake up, but the dark edges hang around, dragging the music back down with it, kicking and screaming; perhaps this encounter was a false dawn. Mirall manages to retain a balanced feel despite its varied instrumentation, while the surprising and utterly gorgeous acapella of ‘Map of Mirrors’ leaves the listener gasping for air. The sublime song is a clearing, an ending, and the start of a new chapter, all at the same time. Heather Woods Broderick’s vocals are drawn-out and peaceable, producing an endless, golden stream that closes the album and signals the coming dawn. www.sonicpieces.com
items._genre: electronic / dark jazz / ambient / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: Rauelsson 的第二张专辑《Mirall》由 Sonic Pieces 厂牌发行，构建了一个夜行性的声景空间。整张作品以连续的整体形式展开，融合了有机驱动的节拍、幽暗的电子音色与丰富的原声乐器编排，包括单簧管、钢琴与弦乐。评论以夜驾穿城的意象贯穿始终，形容其音乐具有暗爵士的气质，在缓慢巡航的节奏中实现了电子段落与器乐段落的无缝衔接。《Mistral》一曲的弦乐提供了短暂的透亮时刻，而 Heather Woods Broderick 在《Map of Mirrors》中的人声则作为全作的收束，以绵延而平和的声线暗示黎明的到来。整体在多样化的乐器编制下保持着统一的氛围平衡。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张在比利时帕克修道院录制、耗时三年完成的群辑合集，汇集十三支比利时乐团的器乐作品。修道院的石质空间与古老壁画成为音乐人的直接灵感来源，自然混响塑造出温暖声响。专辑横跨多个传统：斯洛文尼亚裔小提琴家 Rénélíus Bikar 演绎泛欧罗姆历史；Charlotte Pelgen 与 Bipolar Bows 以尤克里里呈现 Django Reinhardt 风格的爵士摇摆；黎巴嫩裔歌手 Amber Haddad 携乌德琴与低音提琴编织地中海与阿拉伯色彩；Andries Boone 以曼陀林与羽管键琴组合营造近乎巴洛克的室内乐质感；Enara Navaira 则结合喉音唱法与匈牙利 Citera 琴。Airboxes 的手风琴二重奏呈现即兴印象。整张专辑风格虽广，却因共享的灵性空间与制作理念保持内在统一，是一张兼具探索性与沉思气质的跨界世界音乐作品。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦俄罗斯占领下约两万乌克兰儿童被强制带离家园的战争罪行，以音乐为载体回应这一沉重议题。乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka在两国分别组建音乐团队，主要使用弓弦乐器，辅以班杜拉琴、钢琴和双陶笛，呈现传统与现代的交织。曲目既有改编自乌克兰传统的劳工民谣，也有原创作品，通过母女对唱的形式将历史创伤与当下现实并置。部分作品如《Rusalka》转向激烈粗粝的声音质感，与同名水泽精灵的仪式性传统相呼应。乐评指出专辑在音乐和人声层面具有坚实水准，并描述了阅读歌词说明后的强烈情感冲击。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦圣多美和普林西比这一非洲最小岛国之一在七八十年代录制的音乐，核心风格Puxa融合了葡萄牙语非洲殖民地传统节奏与加勒比梅伦格、苏库斯、本加等多种元素。专辑收录超过15首作品，吉他交织缠绕、人声与旋律交织应答，大量曲目以鼓和吉他的律动驱动，展现出适合长时间现场演奏的催眠般律动。Pedro Lima带领乐队以闷音吉他和鼓组对峙，Africa Negra的曲目则以人声退场后的器乐延伸展开。整体呈现的是一个在录音工业不发达的小岛国中依然活跃的音乐生态，节奏层叠、律动狂野，融合跨大西洋音乐传统却保有独特的地方性表达。来自非洲小众地区的世界音乐集合，独立厂牌Bongo Joe发行，具有一定的跨文化探索价值。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典小提琴家与两位挪威音乐家组成三重奏，对斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材进行重新诠释。乐评指出，尽管素材源自传统舞曲，但演奏方式更接近室内乐般的亲密对话，三位乐者沉浸在即兴式的音乐交流中，并非为舞蹈伴奏，而是探索音乐深层含义与隐藏的暗流。专辑以挪威塞特斯达尔山谷的小提琴曲《Fossgrimen》开场，呼应民间传说中瀑布精灵传授琴艺的神话意象，暗示表层欢愉之下的不安底色。在《Polska from Per Myhr》等曲目中，竖笛先行铺垫纹理，小提琴随后引入旋律并以齐奏展开，短小精炼的篇幅内即走向碎片化与停歇，留下大量留白与未完成的张力。整体制作呈现出北欧民间传统与现代实验语汇交织的独特美学。

items._cn_summary: 加拿大作曲家Nicola Miller与德国萨克斯演奏家Frank Gratkowski、鼓手Nick Fraser合作的专辑《SPIT!》，在独立厂牌Watch That Ends the Night发行。Miller在创作中运用频谱分析技术，将人声录音转化为具体的音高与四分之一音和声，这一源自当代古典与电子音乐的方法被引入即兴语境。此外，部分曲目采用了某种随机语言生成过程进行结构组织，将文字处理与声音设计相结合。三位音乐家的合作跨越了欧洲自由即兴与北美当代爵士的场景边界，作品兼具谱面精确性与即兴开放性，体现了从声音材料出发的作曲思维。专辑适合对即兴音乐与实验作曲交叉领域有兴趣的听众。

items.body: In this latest instalment of the Secret History of Film Music, Philip Brophy considers how Jon Brion’s music engenders sympathy for the flawed characters in Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025) and Punch-Drunk Love (2002), and Greta Gerwig’s Lady Bird (2017). As discussed in the previous essay in this series, Jonny Greenwood provides an amazing score for Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another (2025). But two pieces by an earlier composer of Anderson’s films bookend the movie: Jon Brion’s “Bunker Bumper” and “Global Bully”. In One Battle After Another, they function as quietly majestic statements of the drive and exhaustion which propel the intergenerational tale of social reparation and familial separation. “Bunker Bumper” uncoils as a disjointed bossa nova: a gently struck bass drum marks time for the snare, hi-hats and cymbals, skipping with a detached, dainty air. Horns and strings entwine like a billowing flag in slow motion. Sometimes the horns are silenced as the strings climb high, as if they’re searching for something. The music feels absent of harmonic progression; it simply surges, even struggles ahead. It plays near the opening as Pat (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Perfidia (Teyana Taylor) and their radical group French 75 attack a border internment camp. The music intones a sad, fatalistic comment on the limited impact of such revolutionary zeal despite the commitment of its participants. The second track “Global Bully” plays at the film’s end. Years later, Pat relaxes at home with his young adult daughter Willa (Chase Infiniti), offspring of Pat and the long absent Perfidia. The domestic scene shows Willa reading a letter from her mother. In a voiceover, Perfidia acknowledges her mistake in deserting Willa, and expresses hope they will one day meet again. Over a lilting percussive pattern, more strings and horns are orchestrated, but here they coalesce around a chordal pattern. The drums call to mind the tinklers of North American tribal shell shakers engaged in ceremonial dances; the orchestra feels like a calming eulogy played at a church service. The piece acquiesces to how the feisty past can dissolve into a depleted present. It concludes with a touching embrace between Pat and Willa. To label the placement of “Global Bully” here as mere closure misses the weight and precision that Brion’s music bestows on the scene. Across Anderson’s first four films, Brion developed a unique modus operandi of embedding music into movies which, arguably, redefined standard operations of ‘scoring’ and ‘accompaniment’. These two Brion tracks in One Battle After Another were recorded and produced 23 years earlier, for Anderson’s Punch-Drunk Love (2002). That film’s sessions saw Brion continually feeding Anderson with ideas, sketches, recordings and even multitrack breakdowns. All were offered not as thorny strictures, but as flexible flotsam to be experimented with, in terms of how their sono-musical character could enhance and shape onscreen characters. How apt that some of these unused tracks surfaced decades later. As Brion has said: “There are lots of [film composers] doing great things, but it comes down to the director’s ‘follow-through’.” A small suite of prepared piano and percussion ensemble pieces makes up a sizable part of the Punch-Drunk Love score. They sound jittery and clackety, like a wooden digestive system attempting to process parts of a drum kit. They initially read as sound effects more than music – a perceptual doubting, enabled by Gary Rydstrom’s deft mix which folds Brion’s trap kit into Christopher Scarabosio’s sound design (who has handled every Paul Thomas Anderson film since). “Le Petit Chateau” and “Hands And Feet” were based on micro-cassette recordings Brion made of Anderson verbally articulating his ideas for rhythms he wanted to use as timing devices for the film’s long tracking shots. The voice of Anderson became the hands of Brion which became the limbs of Barry (Adam Sandler) who discombobulates throughout the movie in arabesques of anxiety. Upon its release, many assumed the film to be a comedy, thanks to Sandler, but the point was there for an attuned audience: mentally unstable people often appear ‘ridiculous’, but to laugh at their pained performance is inhumane, not to mention imperceptive. Brion’s music plays two roles here. The first, through its percussive moments, is to sonorise the synaptic hell of Barry’s panic attacks, and how desperately out of sync he is with his own body and those around him. The second lies in the sumptuous waltzes (“Punch-Drunk Melody”, “Third Floor Hallway”, “Blossoms & Blood”) which spread the wondrous hope Barry glimpses when he falls in love with Lena (Emily Watson). Irrespective of cliche, the luscious orchestral arrangements welcome the couple into a better, dreamier world. Brion’s music is key in distinguishing Punch-Drunk Love from early 2000s romcom saturation. His arrangements are subtly saccharine, influenced by the lush strings found in rock and pop ballads circa the 1970s, arranged by Van Dyke Parks, Jack Nitzsche and Paul Buckmaster. Their sonority affectionately referenced the easy listening sparkle of 1950/60s hi-fi arrangements by Nelson Riddle and Les Baxter, through to Percy Faith and Paul Mauriat. Brion’s encyclopaedic embrace of recorded popular music is felt in his distinctive melodic sensibility: a transatlantic nexus of solo-Beatles songcraft and Laurel Canyon recording. To be clear, the recording studio rules here, not the concert hall. Punch-Drunk Love used vintage microphones for many of its sessions. The film score brims with detail, space and clarity. Following Punch-Drunk Love, non-mainstream cinema forged a strange meld of nerdy empathy, hipster cynicism and feminist angles in ‘relationship dramedies’: David O Russell’s I Heart Huckabees (2004); Charlie Kaufman’s Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind (2004) and Synecdoche, New York (2008); Miranda July’s The Future (2011); Judd Apatow’s This Is 40 (2012) and Trainwreck (2015); and Greta Gerwig’s Lady Bird (2017). These films cannily merged po-faced ridicule with heartfelt feeling, to varying degrees of success. Yet in all these titles, Brion’s music fortifies their narratives with an endearing romantic sensibility earned by their dysfunctional, antisocial and ‘spectrum’ characters. His Canyon-esque saunter and rich instrumental layering ameliorates any dismissive urges the films’ characters elicit. In Lady Bird, the titular lead (Saoirse Ronan) feels intentionally unlikeable. Equally deliberate is how Brion’s score waltzes around Lady Bird’s teen sense of independence. The film concludes with Lady Bird finally on her own, enrolled in a New York college. At a public phone, she leaves a message for her mother, admitting the rupturing effects of her teen angst created a wedge between them. Brion performs the resonant piano theme like a silent movie accompanist: trilling high notes and copying what’s happening on screen while allowing it space. Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind features similar piano themes played over scenes with onscreen dialogue mixed low. This isn’t simply a formal sonic device: it displaces the viewer/auditor from the psychic space of the story – where you identify or read what’s happening to characters on screen – and relocates you within the characters’ headspace. Positioned this way, the audience can feel a touch exposed, implicated in being present when characters are at their most vulnerable. “Global Bully” fades up in One Battle After Another as we see Lockjaw (Sean Penn) gassed and hear Pat prepare Willa for Perfidia’s letter: death and life fused through emotive exhalation. That seems to be a throughline in the work Brion has provided across the film and music industries. In discussions with Anderson, Brion noted the aim of Punch-Drunk Love was to “feel like a musical, but nobody ever breaks into song”. Brion’s music – and his tremulous voice which has appeared in songs in many of the films mentioned – is similarly shaped by repression, tension and elation, in a fountain of emotional surges. Musical theatre sceptics mostly react against the unbridled emotionalism of onscreen characters liberated from their realistic surroundings. Yet this transcendental effect functions perfectly in recorded songs and popular music in general, generating one of music’s prime private pleasures. Brion and his collaborators have long embraced how song sonics skilfully embedded in the production of a film score can be exhilaratingly transgressive. Wire subscribers can read Philip Brophy’s original Secret History of Film Music columns from the 1990s online in the digital archive. It was revived in 2025 as an online column: previous instalments published on The Wire website can be read here. Wire readers and print and digital subscribers can also find this essay on page 16 of The Wire 512.

items.album: TOM PENAGUIN Tom Penaguin II (Canterbury Scene, 2026)
items.excerpt: Review by BrufordFreak — On his Bandcamp page's "liner notes" Tom lists his "Gear used":Fender Rhodes Mk2 (1, 2, 3, 6)Hohner Pianet C (1, 3, 6)Hohner Cembalet I (1, 3, 6)Columbia Elepian (1)Hammond L122 (1, 3, 4, 5, 6)Roland SH2000 (1, 3, 6)SeagullS12 (1, 3, 6)Gibson SG (1, 6)Gibson Les Paul Goldtop (1, 4)Jacobacci LJ612 double neck (1, 2, 3, 6)Fender JazzbassYamaha Rydeen drumkit1. "Didier Dandelion in the Year of the Great Winds" (13:24) sophisticated, more serious Canterbury Style music
items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — On his Bandcamp page's "liner notes" Tom lists his "Gear used":Fender Rhodes Mk2 (1, 2, 3, 6)Hohner Pianet C (1, 3, 6)Hohner Cembalet I (1, 3, 6)Columbia Elepian (1)Hammond L122 (1, 3, 4, 5, 6)Roland SH2000 (1, 3, 6)SeagullS12 (1, 3, 6)Gibson SG (1, 6)Gibson Les Paul Goldtop (1, 4)Jacobacci LJ612 double neck (1, 2, 3, 6)Fender JazzbassYamaha Rydeen drumkit1. "Didier Dandelion in the Year of the Great Winds" (13:24) sophisticated, more serious Canterbury Style music of the NATIONAL HEALTH sort. A lot of displaying of some mighty fine drumming beneath/within a multi-keyboard vamp. There is a lot of very immersive melodic music here. The multi-instrumentalist seems hell-bent on proving to the world his skills and talents on guitars and keyboards, too. (He is pretty good!) All in all, this is pretty good if sounding a bit like an extension of the 1970s Phil Miller-Dave Stewart-David Sinclair expressions of sophisticated Canterbury Jazz Fusion. The music of this song doesn't always propel--doesn't always feel as if it's moving forward (which was, when I think about it, one of the frequent failings/flaws of the Canterbury artist's music)--but it is an excellent rendering of that era's sound and style. And don't miss the nod to TONY BANKS/Genesis in the "Mad Man Moon" reference in the ninth and tenth minutes as well as the excellent Phil Miller guitar work--which later turns into near-ALLAN HOLDWORTH stuff!--as well as Tom's great drumming. (27.5/30)2. "Mandatory Intermission" (3:47) a piece that feels like a true nod to the most unique genius of the Jazz-Rock Fusion movement: Allan Holdsworth. Even when Tom chooses to settle back into a fuzzy electric guitar over gentle-yet-erudite J-R F band support the lead and music carries with it a kind of reverent "history" of the many stages of growth of the great jazz guitarist: from Bradbury to 'Igginbottom to Nucleus to The Soft Machine up unto the Tempest Jean-Luc Ponty era. Nice homage! (9/10)3. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 1st Movement" (5:21) a Canterbury-inspired weave of bass, drums, electric piano, and guitar that shifts in tempo and dominant (most forward) instrument/sounds between several motifs, including one that introduces a bunch of different keyboard and guitar sounds (including 12-string guitar) while allowing electric bass and drums to remain fairly consistent. I am very much reminded of ANTHONY PHILLIPS and even MIKE RUTHERFORD with a lot of the soundscapes, melodies, and thematic shifts. There's even a little Mike Oldfield in some of the nostalgic melodies and instrumental sound choices, but when Maureen Peircy's "The Northettes'" vocals enter at 4:21 I'm totally taken off guard. Part of me is offended that someone would so blatantly "lift", copy, or replicate such a sacred element of the Canterbury tradition. At the same time, I so welcome and enjoy the brief exposures to the sounds and stylings of these old guys. (9/10)4. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 2nd Movement" (5:35) more Canterbury homage and comfort food. It's as if AI were asked to write some new Dave Stewart (Egg, Khan, Hatfield & The North, National Health) music. It's just too perfect, too much like a re-animation of the old guys: even the production values feel as if I'm listening to some newly-found tapes from 1975 (probably found under the floorboards of the old seaside Wyatt cottage in Lydden [Wellington House]--or better yet--found inside a hash cache inside the walls of Daevid Allen's Bananamoon Observatory in Dei� [Majorca]). I love it while at the same time find myself squirming uncomfortably at the "authentic" feel and sound of the music. I absolutely LOVE hearing more of the peak Canterbury style sound palette--especially when it is rendered so faithfully and so lovingly as this, but more: this is just a great piece of music no matter who did it (or when it was done). (9.25/10)5. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 3rd Movement" (6:18) this one's a little different: harkening back to some of the more sophisticated, mathematical "thought experiments" that Dave Stewart might have had back in the 1970s. There is a feeling of aloneness, even reclusiveness to this piece--even with the participation of the ghosts of Mont Campbell and Clive Brooks (or Richard Sinclair and Robert Wyatt) playing bass and drums, respectively. Even the classical music-mirroring three-part construction harkens back to the work and style of Mont Campbell's EGG trio. Though this replicates some of the early Canterbury music that I am not as attached to as others, I do appreciate its faithful replication of the sound and spirit of one of my all-time favorite eras of music. (8.875/10)6. "The Ornamental Hermit Suite, 4th Movement" (11:50) more modern replication of the sounds and spirit of the uniquely "Canterbury" style geniuses of the 1970s composed, performed, and rendered with truly loving detail. The organ chordplay in the movement's opening minute so remind me of the genius mathematical musings of the great Dave Stewart that I almost tear up. After the 90-second intro enter piano, drums, bass, and electric guitar, gearing up into a real rip-roarer of woven tongues of flame. In the fourth minute the quartet takes a sharp turn down one of the country roads as if on a long descent from the high ground down toward the sea and its beaches and waves--where everything smooths out and soothes the soul. Here Tom chooses to introduce the lead guitar: and lo! and behold! It's Mike Oldfield (or, at least, the ghost-spirit of). I love the infusion in this piece of riffs and stylings from other realms of 1970s prog: Mike Oldfield's guitar in the sixth and seventh minutes, Tony Banks' electric piano sound and stylings, even some sound and chord play that is a nod to Jean-Luc Ponty (in the eighth minute). There is definitely genius (as well as infinite reverence) in this man's compulsion to create (and re-create) music of the artists and magical eras gone by. I find it hard to find fault with this amazing rendering. It even ends with the sound of the tolling of the church bells of some ancient gothic church as if to re-affirm the timeless and universal place that these musics have in our lives. (23/25)Total time: 45:51A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of lovingly-replicated Canterbury Style music. If you love the era, the unique sound and style of those mythical Rainbow artists, you will find yourself melting to the music on this album. Highly recommended.

items._cn_summary: Tom Penaguin II 是一张由多乐器演奏者独立完成的坎特伯雷风格专辑，涉及Fender Rhodes、Hammond L122、Roland SH2000等多种复古键盘与吉他。开篇曲时长十三分钟，以多键盘循环为底，鼓技精湛，整体呈现七十年代Phil Miller、Dave Stewart一脉的精致爵士融合气质，并穿插对Tony Banks及Allan Holdsworth的致敬段落。第二首继续以Holdsworth风格致敬，展现从早期Soft Machine到Tempest时期的演变脉络。第三首套曲在键盘、贝斯、鼓的交织中频繁变换主导乐器与人声段落，旋律带有Anthony Phillips与Mike Oldfield式的怀旧色彩。乐评整体肯定其对坎特伯雷传统的精准还原与乐器驾驭能力，但也指出部分段落推进感不足、过于依赖复古音色而缺乏当代突破。

items.body: “En La Mar”, one of the best loved songs in the Ladino repertoire and one that also travels under the name “La Sirena”, strands a maiden alone in a tower above the sea, calling to the sailors going past, wanting love and wanting out. Rachel Valfer sings her in the Judeo-Spanish that Sephardic Jews took with them when Spain expelled them in 1492 and the Ottoman Empire gave them shelter. David Mac Lean‘s flamenco guitar brings Andalusia back to the song, and the players around it mark where the song went instead: Dan Cantrell on accordion, Faisal Zedan on Arabic percussion, Eliyahu Sills on upright bass and on the bansuri he has played with the group since their first album in 2009. The track comes from Entre Las Huertas, released on 28 August, the third album by the Bay Area’s Qadim Ensemble and the first given over entirely to Ladino. Most of it comes from the kantigas, the songs Sephardic women kept and handed on, so the record runs through lullabies, a wedding party number and a mother unloading about her straying husband while she rocks the baby to sleep. Valfer and Sills have run the group from Berkeley for close to twenty years, she singing in seven languages after six years studying maqam and Persian dastgah in Israel and Palestine, he moving between ney, oud and bass. For this album they went into the studio and played, cutting most of the record live before guests came in with flamenco guitar and qanun. Stream “En La Mar” HERE and take home Entre Las Huertas through THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: The Qadim Ensemble x Rachel Valfer x Eliyahu Sills – En La Mar appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以拉迪诺语（Ladino）为核心语言，呈现了1492年西班牙驱逐犹太人后散居至奥斯曼帝国的塞法迪犹太音乐传统。曲目多源自kantigas——由塞法迪女性世代相传的歌曲，涵盖摇篮曲、婚礼歌谣及生活叙事。专辑以现场录音为主，核心编制包括手风琴、阿拉伯打击乐、低音提琴与bansuri横笛，并邀请弗拉门戈吉他与卡龙琴客串，形成塞法迪传统与安达卢西亚、阿拉伯及印度音乐语汇的跨文化对话。主唱Valfer使用朱德欧-西班牙语演唱，融合了maqam调式研究背景，将犹太离散叙事置于海湾地区的当代音乐实践中。作为一支运营近二十年的团体，这是他们第三张专辑，首次完全聚焦于拉迪诺曲目，展现了女性歌谣传统的延续与跨地域音乐融合的深度。

items.body: Buenos Aires netlabel Cyclical Dreams releases the various-artists compilation “Gemstones VII” on 11 September 2026, the seventh volume of a Berlin School and ambient series the label has issued every September for at least the past three years. The 14-track collection sets contributors from the label’s own artist roster alongside outside acts, working in synthesizer-built ambient, space music and sequenced Berlin School electronics. The ‘Gemstones VII’ tracklist mixes label regulars with outside contributors The album opens with Antike Elektronische Musik’s “Quantum Atlas – Origin” and Alexander Obukhov, recording as Obukhovaudio, on “Plasmadrom”, followed by Wolfgang Merx’s “In Blue” and X-Orbital’s “Timeless Dust Becoming Light”. Aura Merlin contributes “Echo Location”, and Carolyn Fok, whose album “Chrysalis” appeared on Memoir of Sound in 2025, submits “A Leap of Heart (Origin Mix)”. AeTopus adds “Others”, and Cartas de Japón, the band shared by Cyclical Dreams’ three founders, contributes “Faune III”. The second half runs spaceseer’s “Cliffdwellers”, Sophos’s “From Another Time”, and Rodrigo Passannanti‘s “Submerged Industry”, before Kirk Monteux Mysoftmusic’s “Flute Ocean Peace”, the Klaus Wolfe & Castle Waters collaboration “Spirit Bridge”, and Adeptus Mechanicus’s closing “A New Mysterious Beginning”. Cyclical Dreams describes the release as “a walk through beautiful pieces of electronic music inspired by the Berlin School and Ambient music”. Gemstones VII by Various Cyclical Dreams also posted a full-album stream of “Gemstones VII” on its own YouTube channel. “Gemstones VII” follows “Gemstones VI”, released 19 September 2025, and “Gemstones V”, released 13 September 2024, each edition landing in the same week of September for three years running. Side-Line has previously covered Cyclical Dreams releases from D*Time, whose album “Nightwoven” came out on the label in May 2026, and from Christian Wittman, whose album “Andromeda” appeared on Cyclical Dreams in January 2026. About Cyclical Dreams Cyclical Dreams is a netlabel founded in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in early 2020 by musicians Pablo Bilbao, Lucas Tripaldi and Esteban Menash, set up as an outlet for Berlin School, ambient, soundscape, space music and drone electronic music. The three founders play together as Cartas de Japón and also release solo material, including Bilbao’s Pabellón Sintético project and Menash’s M3NASH. Beyond its own roster of artists, Cyclical Dreams runs a Bandcamp store and digital distributor, a mastering service, and the online Cyclical Magazine. The label’s artist roster includes Sophos, the recording name of Argentine composer Ulises Labaronnie, who has worked in music composition and production for 28 years, including the project triØN, film and theatre scores, and music for Cartoon Network video games, alongside concerts in Argentina, Chile and France. Cyclical Dreams has built its “Gemstones” compilation series around annual, dated volumes carrying its own CYD catalog numbers, with “Gemstones V” and “Gemstones VI” preceding this year’s “Gemstones VII” in successive Septembers. The new compilation continues that yearly pattern while again combining the label’s core contributors with outside artists.

items._cn_summary: Cyclical Dreams 厂牌发布第七张合辑，汇集14位艺术家，风格聚焦柏林学派的序列电子、空间音乐与合成器氛围。曲目涵盖多家厂牌内外音乐人，如 Antike Elektronische Musik、Obukhovaudio、Aura Merlin、Carolyn Fok、AeTopus 等，作品多为氛围与序列电子的融合。该厂牌位于阿根廷布宜诺斯艾利斯，由三位创始人于2020年建立，主理人还组成 Cartas de Japón 乐队。该合辑延续了每年九月发行的惯例，内容为不同艺术家对柏林学派与氛围音乐的各自诠释，呈现多样化的电子音乐面貌。作为独立小厂牌发行，音乐探索方向清晰，但合辑形式使得风格统一性和实验深度有限，更多是厂牌生态的一次集中展示。

items.body: Laibach release “MUSICK : ENCORE” on Mute on 20 November 2026, on vinyl, CD and digitally. The companion piece to this year’s “MUSICK” combines unreleased material from the original album sessions with new remixes from SILVERWINGKILLER, Richard X, The Lincolnshire Poacher and PUNCHBAG. MUSICK : ENCORE by Laibach The album leads with two new tracks. “This Is The End” features Slovenian singer Kaja Skrbinšek, while a new version of “Love Machine,” featuring Balkan vocalist Senidah, is remixed by Mute labelmates PUNCHBAG. Senidah also appears on a second version of “Love Machine,” remixed by UK producer The Lincolnshire Poacher. Electropop producer Richard X co-produced several album tracks and remixes “Resistencia,” which also features MRFY member Gregor Strasbergar. Ghanaian artist Wiyaala, whom Laibach first saw performing in an underground club in Ljubljana, appears on two new versions of “Musick”: the Unsick version and a remix by the band’s own guitarist, Vitja Balžalorsky, credited here as Balžalorsky. Long-time Laibach vocalist Marina Mårtensson features on new track “#US,” which SILVERWINGKILLER also remixes, and on “Faith No More” alongside Joker Out guitarist Bojan Cvjetićanin. Koala Voice frontwoman Manca Trampuš features on new track “Modern Talking.” The vinyl edition carries a 10-track selection; the CD and digital editions expand to 13 tracks with the additional remixes. The digital and CD tracklist: “This Is The End” (feat. Kaja Skrbinšek), “Yom Kippur,” “#US” (feat. Marina Mårtensson), “Tales From The Crypt,” “Faith No More” (feat. Marina Mårtensson and Bojan Cvjetićanin), “Musick” (feat. Wiyaala) (Unsick version), “Resistencia” (feat. Gregor Strasbergar) (Richard X remix), “Love Machine” (feat. Senidah) (PUNCHBAG remix), “#US” (feat. Marina Mårtensson) (SILVERWINGKILLER remix), “Modern Talking” (feat. Manca Trampuš), “Allgorhythm” (feat. Wiyaala) (Algorithm remix, assisted by iTurk), “Love Machine” (feat. Senidah) (The Lincolnshire Poacher remix) and “Musick” (feat. Wiyaala) (Balžalorsky remix). “Yom Kippur” previously appeared as a standalone single featuring the Palestinian Children’s Choir, released in October 2025. On the new material, Laibach state: “Perhaps these are the final moments when creating music purely for enjoyment still carries broader significance – before alien, generative intelligence outplays and outperforms us all. So, we seized the moment.” Laibach tour dates for 2026 Laibach continue the “MUSICK” tour through the autumn with UK and European dates, including a show at London’s Islington Assembly Hall on 29 September: 25 September – Ljubljana (SI), Kino Šiška 26 September – Ljubljana (SI), Kino Šiška 29 September – London (UK), Islington Assembly Hall 30 September – Manchester (UK), Ritz 1 October – Southampton (UK), 1865 2 October – Canterbury (UK), The Gulbenkian 4 October – Gent (BE), Democrazy 6 October – Bochum (DE), Zeche 7 October – Nijmegen (NL), Doornroosje 8 October – Hamburg (DE), Große Freiheit 36 9 October – Oslo (NO), Rockefeller Music Hall 11 October – Copenhagen (DK), Bremen Teater 13 October – Berlin (DE), Huxleys Neue Welt 14 October – Dresden (DE), Reithalle 15 October – Brno (CZ), Fleda 16 October – Zagreb (HR), Boogaloo Further European dates are scheduled into 2027, including Milan, Bologna, Lausanne, Paris, Nancy, Winterthur, Vienna, Budapest, Bucharest, Thessaloniki, Athens and Benidorm. About Laibach Laibach formed in 1980 in the mining town of Trbovlje, Slovenia, evolving out of Dejan Knez’s earlier band Salto Mortale. The group co-founded the Neue Slowenische Kunst art collective with the IRWIN and Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre groups in 1984. Their name was officially banned in Yugoslavia in 1983 after a controversial television appearance, a ban lifted in 1985 following the release of their second album, “Nova Akropola,” on Cherry Red Records. Laibach signed to Mute Records for their 1987 album “Opus Dei,” which paired subversive cover versions of Opus’s “Live Is Life” and Queen’s “One Vision” with original material, and went on to release “Let It Be” (1988), “Kapital” (1992) and “NATO” (1994), the latter reworking “The Final Countdown” and other pop and military anthems. The band’s best-known lineup – Milan Fras on vocals, Dejan Knez, Ervin Markošek and Ivan “Jani” Novak – carried Laibach through the 1990s and 2000s, spanning albums including “Jesus Christ Superstars” (1996), “WAT” (2003) and “Volk” (2006). Knez left the group in 2003. More recent studio work includes “Spectre” (2014), “Also Sprach Zarathustra” (2017), “The Sound of Music” (2018), “Wir sind das Volk (ein Musical aus Deutschland)” (2022) and the symphonic work “Alamut” (2022), alongside “Sketches from the Red District” and the “Love Is Still Alive” EP, both from 2023. Milan Fras remains lead vocalist, joined by Ivan “Jani” Novak, longtime vocalist and guitarist Marina Mårtensson and guitarist Vitja Balžalorsky. Recent singles have included covers of “Strange Fruit,” “White Christmas” and Bijelo Dugme’s “Top,” released as “Die Kanone” with Goran Bregović in 2025, plus the “Yom Kippur” single that October. Laibach unveiled “Musick” ahead of its 2026 release on Mute, the group’s most pop-leaning album to date. “MUSICK : ENCORE” extends that record with new songs and remixes, arriving 20 November 2026.

items.body: Soft Vein All We’ve Known of Heaven Artoffact Records If you’ve been following Los Angeles’ Soft Vein since their first LP in 2023 but hadn’t heard any of the pre-release singles for new album All We’ve Known of Heaven you might be forgiven for wondering if it’s even the same project. It’s not that Justin Chamberlain has entirely changed his approach to music: you’re still getting a lot of the same melancholic melodies of the project’s debut and sophomore records, but with the hyper-gloomy and often dour mood of those albums replaced with a powerful, hopeful yearning. Coupled with Chamberlain’s rapid growth as a songwriter, All We’ve Known of Heaven has emerged as one of year’s most moving and engaging listens. Chamberlain’s biggest asset in both his songcraft and his performances is his sense of restraint. The album’s feeling of intimacy comes directly from how simultaneously laidback and vulnerable it comes across; a cut like “Forgetting You” works because its clean, Knopfler-esque guitar and multi-tracked vocals bring you in, setting you up for the big drum machine claps and a damnably catchy chorus. The effect is that it feels like the songs being sung to you as a listener, not at you. When Chamberlain asks “Is this all we are?/All we know?” on the jaw-dropping synthpop gem “All We’ve Known of Heaven” it’s a question directed at the world at large, its ruminations on the sad state of things in the early days of the 21st century building to a plea for a kinder, more loving world. It’s stirring by virtue of the honesty with which it’s delivered, both vocally and musically, from its tasteful synthwork and the smooth closing saxophone solo, to the cathartic introspection of its lyrics and Chamberlain’s deeply heartfelt vocals. The warmth and passion of the songs are fully supported by the wonderfully lush and refined production from Chamberlain himself, assisted by live member Andrea Mantione of Nuovo Testamento. “Learning to Talk” is a sweet love song about the sense of discovery in being with another person, its little synth and guitar trills and half-whispered opening verse building momentum gradually, the space around the instruments growing into a powerful climax. In one of the record’s best moments on “Chekhov”, the edge of bitterness and disappointment in Chamberlain’s voice is perfectly matched by the ghostly pads that hang behind him like a reminder, suggesting a soft but everpresent ache. Similarly, the Cocteau Twins guitars that adorn “White Towers (White Shores)” work so well because the song’s programmed drums and keys are locked in beneath them, lifting the song up while also pushing it forwards. All We’ve Known of Heaven is comforting, quietly confident, unhurried, and above all an incredibly lovely record to just sit and listen to. Justin Chamberlain’s willingness to let the songs speak for themselves is certainly a part of it; while no doubt there’s passion and investment in every moment of the LP, it’s all presented with an unpretentious and open candor that makes it easy to get swept up in its grand swells of emotion. An absolute stunner of a album, and one of the year’s best to date. Recommended. Buy it. All We've Known of Heaven by Soft Vein The post Soft Vein, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: Soft Vein的第二张专辑展现了从早期阴郁沉闷氛围向温暖渴望的明显转变，核心在于创作人Justin Chamberlain在旋律写作上的克制与亲密感。清亮的吉他音色与多轨人声构建出贴近听众的叙事距离，合成器音色考究，萨克斯独奏增添了舒缓的层次。制作由Chamberlain本人与Nuovo Testamento成员Andrea Mantione共同完成，注重空间感与渐进式张力。歌词围绕21世纪初人类境况展开思索，呼唤一个更友善的世界，情感表达真挚而内省。歌曲结构多采用渐进式构建，从低语式的开场逐步推向高潮。整体呈现出舒适、不急不躁、安静的自信气质，适合静坐聆听。
